questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Which question can a scientist answer by collecting evidence?
options: Does a bigger sail make a toy boat go faster?
Which colour of boat is the prettiest?
Is sailing more fun than swimming?
Do boats look nicest on a river?
questions.explanation: A testable question can be answered with measurements or observations. Questions about what is prettiest, nicest or most fun are opinions, so a test cannot settle them.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Match each measurement to the unit you would normally use.
pairs: the mass of a bag of rice
the time of a rickshaw ride
the volume of milk in a jug
questions.explanation: Choosing the right unit matters: mass is in grams or kilograms, force in newtons, time in seconds or minutes, volume in millilitres or litres, temperature in °C and loudness in decibels.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: In a fair test you change ___ thing, measure one thing and keep everything else the ___.
questions.explanation: If you change two things at once you cannot tell which one caused the result. The things you keep the same are called control variables.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Repeating a measurement and working out the mean makes your results more reliable.
questions.explanation: One measurement can contain a mistake. Repeating (often three times) and finding the mean gives results you can trust more, and it helps you spot an odd result.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Mina asks: "Does the amount of water change how tall bean seedlings grow?" Sort each item into its job in the investigation.
questions.explanation: Mina changes only the amount of water (independent variable) and measures the height (dependent variable). Everything else must stay the same so the test is fair.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: To find the mean of 8, 10 and 12, add them up and ___ the total by 3. The mean is ___.
questions.explanation: 8 + 10 + 12 = 30, and 30 ÷ 3 = 10. To find a mean, add the results and divide by how many results there are.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Choose the best graph for each set of results.
items: number of children who walk, cycle or take a bus to school
mass of a mango, a banana and a guava
water held by sand, soil and clay
height of a bean plant measured every day
temperature of a pot of water as it is heated each minute
length of a shadow measured every hour
questions.explanation: Use a bar chart when the thing you changed is in groups or words. Use a line graph when it is a number that changes smoothly, such as time.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Match each investigation to its type of enquiry.
pairs: Which kind of paper towel soaks up the most water?
Measuring a puppy's mass every week
Do taller children have longer feet?
Sorting shells into groups by shape
Using books to find out how the first aeroplane flew
questions.explanation: Scientists choose the type of enquiry that suits the question: a fair test changes one variable, while other enquiries watch change, look for patterns, sort things or use secondary sources.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Put the steps of a scientific investigation in order.
sequence: Ask a question that can be tested.
Make a prediction and give a reason.
Plan the test and decide what to keep the same.
Measure and record the results in a table.
Draw a graph and look for a pattern.
Write a conclusion and say how to improve.
questions.explanation: Good investigations follow a clear path: question, prediction, plan, results, pattern, and finally a conclusion with an evaluation.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Mina watches a bean seed germinate in a clear jar for a week. Which observations are the most useful? Choose all that are right.
options: On day 3 the seed coat splits and a root appears.
The shoot is 2 cm tall on day 5.
A lizard walked past the window.
The jar stands on the left of the shelf.
The root grows downwards and the shoot grows upwards.
questions.explanation: Useful observations describe the change you are studying, with numbers and times when possible. The lizard and the jar's position have nothing to do with germination.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: A model of the Solar System small enough to fit on a desk shows the real sizes and distances of the planets correctly.
questions.explanation: Models are useful but have limitations. To fit on a desk, the planets and their distances must be changed in scale, so the real Solar System is far bigger and emptier.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Which is the best heading for a column of times in a results table?
options: Time
How fast
Time (s)
Fast or slow
questions.explanation: A table heading says what was measured and gives the unit, such as Time (s). Then the numbers in the column do not need units.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Why did Jagadish Chandra Bose invent the crescograph?
options: To weigh leaves more exactly.
To make plants grow faster.
To measure how loud plants are.
To magnify plant movements too small to see.
questions.explanation: Plant growth and movement are far too small and slow to see. The crescograph magnified them about 10 000 times, so Bose could collect new evidence and show that plants react to light, heat, touch and chemicals.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Raju wants to predict: "Will a puddle dry faster in the sun or in the shade?" Which is the best prediction?
options: It will dry faster in the shade because shade makes water lighter.
It will dry faster in the sun because heat makes water evaporate faster.
It will dry faster in the sun because I like sunny days.
It will dry at the same speed because all puddles are alike.
questions.explanation: A good prediction says what will happen and gives a reason from science. Warmer water evaporates faster. A liking for sunny days is not a scientific reason.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Read the thermometer scale with your eye level with the mark. What temperature does thermometer B show?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C with different liquid levels on a scale from 0 to 50 degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: The liquid in thermometer B stops at 25 °C, halfway between the 20 and 30 marks. Always read the mark level with the top of the liquid.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Look at the three thermometers. The difference between the highest and the lowest reading is ___ °C.
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C with different liquid levels on a scale from 0 to 50 degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: The highest reading is thermometer C at 48 °C and the lowest is thermometer A at 12 °C. 48 − 12 = 36 °C.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Rafi hangs a bag from the forcemeter. What is the reading, with the correct unit?
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter with a spring, a pointer and a scale from 0 to 10.
options: 4 g
4 N
3 N
questions.explanation: The pointer is at the 4 mark. Forces are measured in newtons (N), not grams, which are a unit of mass.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: The forcemeter shows ___ N. A second, lighter bag pulls with 4 N, so the first bag pulls ___ N more.
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter with a spring, a pointer and a scale from 0 to 10.
questions.explanation: The pointer is at 7 N. Comparing the bags: 7 − 4 = 3 N more.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Match each tool to what it measures.
questions.explanation: Each tool measures one thing: a balance measures mass, a stopwatch measures time, a thermometer measures temperature and a ruler measures length.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Priya wants to look closely at the tiny veins in a leaf. Which tool should she use?
questions.explanation: A magnifying glass (hand lens) makes small details look bigger, so it helps careful observation. The other tools measure time, length and mass.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Arif wants to know which of three fertilisers helps his chilli plants grow tallest. Which plan is the fairest?
options: Change the fertiliser and the pot size, so he sees which helps most.
Give each plant a fertiliser in the place that looks best.
Change only the fertiliser; give every plant the same soil, pot, water and light.
Use one fertiliser on all plants and change the amount of water.
questions.explanation: A fair test changes only one variable. If Arif changed the pot size or the place as well, he could not tell whether the fertiliser caused the difference.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Tuli wants to find which of four kinds of cloth dries fastest on the clothesline. Which things must she keep the same? Choose all that are right.
options: the size of each cloth
the type of cloth
the amount of water in each cloth
where on the line each cloth hangs
the time taken to dry
questions.explanation: The type of cloth is what Tuli changes, and the time taken to dry is what she measures. Size, water and place are control variables, so they must stay the same.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Joy times a rickshaw crossing a bridge three times with a stopwatch: 62 s, 60 s and 64 s. The mean time is ___ s.
questions.explanation: 62 + 60 + 64 = 186, and 186 ÷ 3 = 62 s. Reporting the mean of three timings is more reliable than reporting one.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Lina feels hot and her mother thinks she has a fever. Which instrument and unit should they use?
options: a stopwatch, in s
a thermometer, in °C
a balance, in g
a measuring cylinder, in ml
questions.explanation: Body temperature is measured with a thermometer in degrees Celsius. The other instruments measure time, mass and volume.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Rafi's father plants a new kind of rice in one corner of his field and the old kind in the rest. The new rice gives more grain, so he says it is better. What is the biggest problem with his test?
options: He should have tested the rice in a laboratory.
He should have used a different fertiliser for each kind.
There is no problem: a bigger harvest always proves a better kind.
The two kinds grew in different places and were tested only once.
questions.explanation: The corner may have better soil or more water, so the place could explain the result. A fair test grows both kinds in the same conditions and repeats the test.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Sumi wants to find out which of three brands of soap washes a muddy cloth cleanest. Describe how she could make it a fair test.
questions.model_answer: Change only the brand of soap. Use cloths of the same size with the same amount of mud, the same amount of soap and water, and the same washing time. Repeat the test three times.
questions.explanation: A fair test changes one variable (the brand), measures one thing (how clean the cloth is) and keeps the cloth, mud, soap, water and time the same. Repeating makes the results more reliable.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Example class experiment: Class 5B dropped a ball from 1 m and measured the bounce height in five tries: 52 cm, 54 cm, 31 cm, 53 cm and 51 cm. In the third try the ball was dropped from a lower height by mistake. What is the best mean to report?
options: 48.2 cm, using all five results
31 cm, the lowest result
52.5 cm, leaving out the 31 cm result
54 cm, the highest result
questions.explanation: The 31 cm result is an anomaly with a known cause, so it is left out. (52 + 54 + 53 + 51) ÷ 4 = 210 ÷ 4 = 52.5 cm. Using all five results gives 48.2 cm, which is pulled down by the mistake.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Example data: a cup of tea was left to cool. At 0, 5, 10 and 15 minutes its temperature was 80 °C, 62 °C, 50 °C and 43 °C. What is the best prediction for 20 minutes?
options: About 25 °C, because it falls by 18 °C every 5 minutes.
About 43 °C, because the tea has stopped cooling.
About 55 °C, because tea warms up again.
About 38 °C, because it keeps cooling but by smaller amounts each time.
questions.explanation: The drops are 18, 12 and 7 °C, so the tea cools more slowly as it gets closer to room temperature. The next drop is smaller still, about 5 °C, giving about 38 °C.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Example data: Imran tested three paper towels. Towel A has 2 layers and soaked up 10 ml of water. Towel B has 3 layers and soaked up 14 ml. Towel C has 4 layers and soaked up 18 ml. Which statements are supported by the data? Choose all that are right.
options: Towel C soaked up the most water.
Each extra layer soaked up about 4 ml more water.
Towels that cost more are always better.
Towel B soaked up less water than towel A.
The colour of the towel changed how much water it soaked up.
questions.explanation: A conclusion must be backed by the results. The table shows C took up the most and that each extra layer added about 4 ml. It says nothing about cost or colour, and B soaked up more than A, not less.

questions.title: The Scientist's Toolkit
questions.stem: Anika predicted that salty water would freeze faster than tap water. Her results showed that the tap water froze first. She says: "My investigation failed because my prediction was wrong." Do you agree? Explain.
questions.model_answer: No, I disagree. A result that does not match the prediction is still useful evidence. Her investigation answered the question, and she can use the results to change her idea and make a new prediction.
questions.explanation: Science is about following the evidence. A surprising result teaches us something and can lead to a better explanation and a new prediction. (Salt really does lower the freezing point of water.)

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Organs that work together to do a big job make up an…
options: artery
nutrient
joint
organ system
questions.explanation: An organ is a body part with a special job. Organs that work together form an organ system, such as the digestive system.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Match each organ to its job.
pairs: helps digestion and cleans the blood
a muscle that helps you breathe
questions.explanation: Each organ has a special job. The windpipe and the oesophagus are both tubes, but one carries air and the other carries food.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Sort each organ into its organ system.
questions.explanation: The digestive system breaks down food, the respiratory system handles breathing, the circulatory system moves blood, and the nervous system carries messages and controls the body.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Rafi touches a hot pan and quickly pulls his hand away. Put the path of the message in order.
sequence: Nerves in the skin of his hand sense the heat.
A message travels along nerves to the spinal cord and brain.
A message is sent back along nerves to the arm.
Muscles in his arm pull the hand away.
questions.explanation: The nervous system carries messages at high speed: in from the sense organ, to the spinal cord and brain, and out again to the muscles.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Food goes from the mouth down the ___ to the stomach. Most nutrients pass into the blood in the ___ intestine.
questions.explanation: The oesophagus (food pipe) carries food to the stomach. The windpipe carries air, and the large intestine mostly takes back water.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Oxygen is the waste gas that we breathe out.
questions.explanation: We breathe in oxygen, which passes into the blood. The waste gas that we breathe out is carbon dioxide.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Which jobs does the skeletal system do? Choose all that are right.
options: holds the body up
protects soft organs such as the brain
works with muscles so we can move
pumps blood around the body
filters the blood to make urine
questions.explanation: Bones support and protect the body and work with muscles for movement. Pumping blood is the heart's job and filtering blood is the kidneys' job.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: What is your pulse?
options: the beat of blood pushed through an artery
the speed of nerve messages in the body
the number of breaths in each minute
the noise of food moving in your gut
questions.explanation: Each time the heart pumps, it pushes blood through the arteries, and you can feel this beat as your pulse, for example on your wrist.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Where is urine stored until you go to the toilet?
options: kidney
liver
bladder
stomach
questions.explanation: The kidneys filter the blood and make urine. The urine is then stored in the bladder.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Match each organ system to its main job.
pairs: takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide
gets rid of waste made by the body
carries messages to control the body
questions.explanation: The six main organ systems each have their own job, and they work together to keep us alive.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Blood flows around the body in tubes called blood ___. The tiniest tubes are called ___.
questions.explanation: Blood vessels are arteries, veins and tiny capillaries. Capillaries reach every part of the body to deliver oxygen and nutrients.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: What does the diaphragm do?
options: It pumps blood to the lungs.
It is a muscle that helps you breathe.
It filters waste from the blood.
It carries air down to the lungs.
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is a sheet of muscle under the lungs that moves to help air go in and out. The heart pumps blood and the windpipe carries air.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Explain how oxygen gets from the air to the muscles in your legs.
questions.model_answer: You breathe air in through your nose and mouth, and it goes down the windpipe to the lungs. Oxygen passes into the blood in the lungs, and the heart pumps the blood around the body to the muscles.
questions.explanation: The respiratory system takes oxygen into the blood, and the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels) carries it to every cell. Both systems are needed.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: The nervous system is made of the brain only.
questions.explanation: The nervous system also includes the spinal cord and the nerves. The sense organs send information to it, and nerves carry messages around the body.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Match each number in the picture to the right bone.
questions.image_alt: A human skeleton with six bones numbered.
questions.explanation: The skull (1) protects the brain, the ribs (2) protect the heart and lungs, the spine (3) holds the body up and protects the spinal cord, and the thigh bone (5) is the longest bone in the body.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Match each organ or group of organs to the numbered part of the body where it is found.
questions.image_alt: An outline of a child with body parts numbered 1 to 11.
questions.explanation: The brain is in the head (1). The heart and lungs are in the chest (7), and the stomach and intestines are in the tummy (8).

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Which number shows a joint, where two bones meet?
questions.image_alt: An arm showing a bone, the biceps, the triceps and the elbow joint, numbered 1 to 4.
questions.explanation: Number 4 is the elbow joint, where the upper arm bone meets the lower arm bones. Numbers 2 and 3 are muscles.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: In the picture, the part numbered 4 protects the brain.
questions.image_alt: A human skeleton with six bones numbered.
questions.explanation: Number 4 is the pelvis, which supports the body and protects organs in the lower tummy. The skull (1) protects the brain.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into the organ system each one belongs to.
questions.explanation: The brain controls the body and the eye is a sense organ that sends messages to it. The lungs are for breathing, the heart pumps blood, and teeth chew food at the start of digestion.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Which numbered part carries messages from the eye to the brain?
questions.image_alt: A cross-section of the eye with parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: The optic nerve (5) is part of the nervous system. It carries messages from the retina (4) to the brain, which makes sense of what we see.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: At sports day Rima runs a race. Her heart beats much faster and she breathes hard. What is the best explanation?
options: Her bones need more blood to stop them breaking.
Her muscles need more oxygen, so breathing and heartbeat speed up.
Her stomach needs to digest her lunch faster.
Her kidneys need to make more urine quickly.
questions.explanation: Working muscles need more oxygen and energy. Faster breathing takes in more oxygen and a faster heartbeat carries it to the muscles more quickly.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: On a winter morning in Dhaka the air quality index (AQI) is 245, which is "very unhealthy" (201–300). What is the best decision for Moung's class?
options: Move sports indoors and wear masks outside.
Open all the windows for fresh air.
Hold sports outdoors as normal.
Run extra laps to make lungs stronger.
questions.explanation: Children breathe faster and deeper when they exercise, so they take in more polluted air. On very unhealthy days it is safer to stay indoors or limit time outside.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: After jogging, Imran counts 22 beats of his pulse in 15 seconds. His pulse rate is ___ beats per minute.
questions.explanation: There are four 15-second periods in one minute, so multiply by 4: 22 × 4 = 88 beats per minute.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Which actions help protect people's lungs in a polluted city? Choose all that are right.
options: wear a mask on very polluted days
spray water on dust at building sites
burn rubbish instead of collecting it
check that vehicles do not give out thick smoke
exercise next to a busy road at rush hour
questions.explanation: Masks, damping down dust and cleaner vehicles all reduce the tiny particles we breathe in. Burning rubbish and exercising beside heavy traffic add to the problem.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: A doctor puts a stethoscope on a child's chest to listen to the heart and lungs. Which two body systems is she checking?
options: digestive and nervous
skeletal and excretory
circulatory and respiratory
excretory and nervous
questions.explanation: The heart belongs to the circulatory system and the lungs belong to the respiratory system. Both are found in the chest.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Nadia lives near a brick kiln in Dhaka and often coughs in winter. Explain how the smoke can harm her body.
questions.model_answer: Tiny particles in the smoke travel deep into her lungs and can cause coughing and lung infections. Some of the particles pass into the blood and can strain the heart, so the respiratory and circulatory systems are harmed.
questions.explanation: The smallest particles (PM2.5) are about 30 times thinner than a human hair. They reach deep into the lungs, and some even enter the blood, so they affect both breathing and the heart.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Example data: Tuli counted her pulse for 15 seconds. She counted 19 beats while resting and 31 beats after jogging. By how many beats per minute did her pulse rise?
options: 12 beats per minute
124 beats per minute
76 beats per minute
48 beats per minute
questions.explanation: Resting: 19 × 4 = 76 beats per minute. After jogging: 31 × 4 = 124 beats per minute. The rise is 124 − 76 = 48. The answer 12 forgets to change 15 seconds into a minute.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: A person can live with only one kidney, but not without a heart. Which explanation is best?
options: Kidneys only store urine, so they are not needed.
One kidney can still filter enough blood, but nothing else can pump blood to the cells.
The heart is bigger, so it does more work than both kidneys.
Kidneys are smaller than the heart, so they matter less.
questions.explanation: One kidney can do the work of two. Without a heartbeat, oxygen and nutrients cannot reach the cells. Kidneys filter blood and make urine; the bladder stores it.

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Example data: a school recorded the AQI each morning: Sat 120, Sun 158, Mon 205, Tue 310, Wed 175. The scale is: 101–150 unhealthy for sensitive groups, 151–200 unhealthy, 201–300 very unhealthy, 301 and above hazardous. Which statements are true? Choose all that are right.
options: The most polluted day was Tuesday, and the air was hazardous.
The air was "unhealthy" or worse on four of the five days.
Saturday's air was in the "very unhealthy" category.
The AQI rose every day.
Wednesday was more polluted than Monday.
questions.explanation: Tuesday (310) is the highest and is 301 or above. Sun, Mon, Tue and Wed are all 151 or more. Saturday (120) was only unhealthy for sensitive groups, and Wednesday (175) fell below Monday (205).

questions.title: Human Body Systems
questions.stem: Joy wrote four statements about the body. Which one is **not** correct?
options: Nutrients pass into the blood in the small intestine.
The heart pumps blood to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen.
The kidneys store urine until it leaves the body.
The ribs protect the heart and lungs.
questions.explanation: The kidneys filter the blood and make urine, but the bladder stores it. The other three statements are correct.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Robert Hooke gave cells their name in 1665 after looking at a thin slice of…
options: onion skin
pond water
blood
cork
questions.explanation: Hooke looked at cork through a microscope and saw rows of tiny boxes that reminded him of small rooms, so he called them cells.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Match each specialised cell to its job.
pairs: gets shorter to move the body
stores energy and helps keep us warm
questions.explanation: Cells in the body are specialised: each kind has a shape that suits its job.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Put the levels of organisation in order from smallest to largest.
sequence: cell
tissue
organ
organ system
organism
questions.explanation: Cells make tissues, tissues make organs, organs work together in organ systems, and all the organ systems together make a whole organism.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: A group of similar cells doing the same job is called a ___. Different tissues working together make an ___.
questions.explanation: Muscle tissue is a group of muscle cells. The heart is an organ because it is made of muscle tissue and other tissues working together.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Most cells are too small to see without a microscope.
questions.explanation: Your body has about 30 trillion cells, and most of them are far too small for our eyes. We need a microscope to see them.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: A tissue is made of many different organs working together.
questions.explanation: A tissue is made of many similar cells doing the same job. It is an organ that is made of different tissues.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Sort each example into its level of organisation.
items: muscle tissue in the heart wall
questions.explanation: A cell is the smallest unit, similar cells form a tissue, tissues form an organ such as the brain, and organs working together form an organ system.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Which parts do animal cells have? Choose all that are right.
options: cell membrane
cell wall
cytoplasm
nucleus
chloroplasts
questions.explanation: Animal cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. The cell wall and chloroplasts are extra parts found in plant cells.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Red blood cells are round and dented in the middle. How does this shape help them?
options: It lets them get shorter to move the body.
It gives a large surface for carrying oxygen.
It lets them store fat for energy.
It lets them send messages along nerves.
questions.explanation: The dented disc shape gives a large surface for carrying oxygen, and the cells can bend to squeeze through tiny blood vessels.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Match each cell shape to the job it helps the cell to do.
pairs: carries messages quickly over long distances
long and able to get shorter
flat and fitting together like tiles
carries oxygen and squeezes through tiny vessels
questions.explanation: In specialised cells the shape fits the job. Long branching nerve cells reach far; tile-like skin cells leave no gaps for germs.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Which part of an animal cell is a thin skin that controls what goes in and out?
options: nucleus
cytoplasm
cell membrane
chloroplast
questions.explanation: The cell membrane holds the cell together and controls what passes in and out. The nucleus is the control centre and the cytoplasm is the jelly where the work happens.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: An animal cell has three main parts: the cell ___, the jelly-like ___ and the ___, which is the control centre.
questions.explanation: The membrane is the thin skin, the cytoplasm is the jelly where the cell's work happens, and the nucleus holds the instructions for the cell.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Explain how the shape of a nerve cell helps it do its job.
questions.model_answer: A nerve cell is long and thin with branches, so it can carry messages quickly over a long distance and connect to many other cells.
questions.explanation: The long, branching shape lets nerve cells carry messages around the body at high speed and pass them on to other cells.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek saw living cells, such as blood cells, that Hooke had not seen. Why was he able to?
options: He made better lenses.
He used a bigger piece of cork.
He looked only at plants.
He could see cells with his eyes alone.
questions.explanation: Leeuwenhoek made better lenses, so he could see much smaller things. A better instrument gave him new evidence, including living cells and tiny creatures in pond water.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Match each number in the picture to the name of the part.
questions.image_alt: An animal cell with three parts numbered 1 to 3.
questions.explanation: The cell membrane (1) is the outer skin, the cytoplasm (2) is the jelly inside and the nucleus (3) is the control centre.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: In the picture, the part numbered 1 is the jelly where the cell's work happens.
questions.image_alt: An animal cell with three parts numbered 1 to 3.
questions.explanation: Part 1 is the cell membrane, the thin skin around the cell. The jelly where the work happens is the cytoplasm, part 2.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: A plant cell has all the parts of this animal cell and also a tough cell wall. Where would the cell wall be?
questions.image_alt: An animal cell with three parts numbered 1 to 3.
options: inside part 3
just outside part 1
inside part 2
instead of part 2
questions.explanation: The cell wall is a strong layer around the outside of a plant cell, just beyond the cell membrane (1). It helps the plant stand up without bones.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Which two numbered parts of the arm are mostly made of muscle tissue? Choose all that are right.
questions.image_alt: An arm showing a bone (1), the biceps (2), the triceps (3) and the elbow joint (4).
questions.explanation: The biceps (2) and triceps (3) are muscles, so they are made of muscle tissue, which is full of muscle cells that can get shorter. Number 1 is a bone and number 4 is a joint.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Is each picture a whole organism or only an organ? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: An organ is one part of a body with a special job. An organism is a whole living thing, such as a cat, a fish or a rice plant.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: All living things are made of cells. Which of these is made of cells?
questions.explanation: A rice plant is a living thing, so it is made of cells. Rocks, coins and plastic bottles were never alive and are not made of cells.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Many children in Bangladesh have thalassaemia and cannot make enough healthy red blood cells. Why might such a child feel tired and weak?
options: Their nerve cells cannot carry messages.
Their skin cells do not fit together.
Less oxygen reaches their cells to release energy.
Their fat cells store too much energy.
questions.explanation: Red blood cells carry oxygen to every cell, and cells need oxygen to release energy from food. With fewer healthy red blood cells, the child has less energy.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: A blood donor at a Sandhani camp gives about 450 ml of blood. An adult has about 5 litres (5000 ml) of blood. About what fraction of the donor's blood was given?
options: about one half
about one quarter
about one hundredth
about one tenth
questions.explanation: 450 ml is close to 500 ml, and 500 ÷ 5000 = one tenth. The body replaces the liquid within a day or two and the red blood cells within a few weeks.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: A poster at a blood donation camp explains what blood is made of. Match each part of blood to its job.
pairs: liquid that carries the cells and nutrients
questions.explanation: Blood is a mixture of cells floating in a yellow liquid called plasma. Each part has its own job.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Anika is going to look at onion skin under a school microscope. What is the safest, correct way to start?
options: Begin with the smallest lens, focus, then try a bigger one.
Begin with the biggest lens so the cells look large.
Point the mirror straight at the Sun to get more light.
Press the slide down hard so it stays still.
questions.explanation: Start with the smallest objective lens, focus, then move up to a bigger one. Never point a microscope mirror at the Sun, and handle glass slides gently.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Priya's microscope has a ×10 eyepiece lens and she uses the ×40 objective lens. The total magnification is ×___.
questions.explanation: Multiply the eyepiece by the objective lens: 10 × 40 = 400. The onion cells look 400 times bigger.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Imran says: "If the heart stops working, only the circulatory system is affected." Is he right? Use what you know about organ systems to explain.
questions.model_answer: He is not right. The heart pumps blood that carries oxygen from the lungs to all the cells, so every organ system would stop working and the whole organism would be in danger.
questions.explanation: Organs and organ systems depend on each other. If the heart stops, oxygen from the lungs cannot reach the cells, so all the other systems fail.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Your body makes about 2 million new red blood cells every second. About how many does it make in 2 minutes?
options: 4 million
24 million
120 million
240 million
questions.explanation: In 1 minute: 2 million × 60 = 120 million. In 2 minutes: 120 million × 2 = 240 million.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Which list shows the levels of organisation for the heart, from smallest to largest?
options: muscle tissue → heart muscle cell → heart → human → circulatory system
heart muscle cell → muscle tissue → heart → circulatory system → human
heart → heart muscle cell → muscle tissue → circulatory system → human
human → circulatory system → heart → muscle tissue → heart muscle cell
questions.explanation: Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism. The last list runs from largest to smallest, and the other two mix up the levels.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: Which statements about cells are true? Choose all that are right.
options: Plant and animal cells both have a nucleus.
Plant cells have a cell wall, but animal cells do not.
The cell membrane holds the instructions that control the cell.
Chloroplasts in plant cells trap light.
All cells in the human body have the same shape.
questions.explanation: The nucleus, not the membrane, holds the instructions. Cells in the body come in different shapes because they have different jobs.

questions.title: Cells, Tissues and Organs
questions.stem: We cannot see a single heart cell with our eyes alone, but we can see a heart. Explain why.
questions.model_answer: A cell is microscopic, too small for our eyes. An organ like the heart is made of millions of cells grouped together into tissues, so it is big enough to see.
questions.explanation: Most cells are far too small to see. But an organ contains millions of cells in groups, so together they make something large enough to see.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: To stay healthy we need clean air and safe ___, good hygiene, nutritious food, ___ and enough sleep.
questions.explanation: A healthy lifestyle needs clean surroundings, clean air, safe water, good hygiene, nutritious food, exercise and enough sleep. When these are missing, people are more likely to become ill.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Sort each disease by the main way it spreads.
questions.explanation: Knowing how a disease spreads shows how to stop it: safe water and food, covering coughs and sneezes, and stopping mosquitoes from breeding.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: All germs cause disease.
questions.explanation: Most germs (microbes) are harmless and some are even useful. Only some of them cause disease.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Diabetes is an infectious disease that spreads from person to person through coughs and sneezes.
questions.explanation: Diabetes does not spread from person to person. Diseases such as diabetes and heart disease are linked to lifestyle, for example too little exercise or too much sugar and fat.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Put the steps of handwashing in the correct order.
sequence: Wet your hands with clean water.
Add soap.
Rub palms, backs of hands and between fingers.
Scrub nails and thumbs.
Rinse well.
Dry with a clean cloth.
questions.explanation: Washing in this order, with soap and for about 20 seconds, removes most germs. Do not forget the thumbs, nails and spaces between the fingers.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Wash your hands with soap for about ___ seconds, especially before eating and after using the toilet.
questions.explanation: Rubbing with soap for about 20 seconds removes most germs. A quick 2 to 5 second rinse leaves many germs behind.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: What does a vaccine do?
options: It replaces the water and salts lost in diarrhoea.
It trains the body to fight a germ.
It kills mosquitoes that come into the home.
It makes the body grow taller and stronger.
questions.explanation: A vaccine trains the body to recognise and fight a germ before it attacks. Bangladesh's vaccination programme protects children from measles, polio and tetanus.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Match each problem to a disease it can cause.
pairs: a bite from an Aedes mosquito
too little exercise and too much sugar
questions.explanation: Unhealthy conditions are linked to diseases. Dirty water carries germs, mosquitoes carry the dengue virus, coughs spread flu, and an unhealthy lifestyle raises the risk of diabetes.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Which habits help to prevent disease? Choose all that are right.
options: wash hands with soap before eating
drink water straight from a pond
empty containers of standing water every week
cough into your open hand
use a clean toilet (latrine)
questions.explanation: Soap, a clean toilet and no standing water all stop germs and mosquitoes. Pond water can carry germs, and coughing into your hand spreads them.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: About how many hours of sleep does a child aged 6 to 12 need each night?
options: 5 to 6 hours
7 to 8 hours
13 to 15 hours
9 to 12 hours
questions.explanation: Children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep to grow, learn and stay well. Sleep also helps the body fight infection.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: A disease that spreads from person to person is ___. A sign of illness, such as a fever or a cough, is a ___.
questions.explanation: Infectious diseases can pass from one person to another. A symptom is a sign that a person is ill.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: A child has diarrhoea and is losing a lot of water. Why is ORS better than plain water?
options: It makes the child feel sleepy for longer.
It gives the body extra fat to store.
It replaces the lost salts as well as water.
It kills all the germs that are inside the body.
questions.explanation: ORS (oral rehydration solution) replaces the salts the body has lost, and its sugar helps the body absorb the salts and water. Scientists in Dhaka helped show how much it can help.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Explain why a vaccine protects other people as well as you.
questions.model_answer: If you are vaccinated you cannot catch the disease, so you cannot pass it on. When many people are vaccinated the germ cannot spread easily, so babies and sick people are protected too.
questions.explanation: A germ needs people to spread between. If most people are vaccinated, it has few people to pass to, which protects even those who cannot be vaccinated.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Dengue is spread by the bite of a mosquito.
questions.explanation: Dengue is caused by a virus that the female Aedes mosquito passes on when it bites. Malaria is also spread by mosquitoes.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Rubbish and dirty water attract some animals that spread germs. Sort the pictures.
categories: Do not spread disease to people
items: Do not spread disease to people
Do not spread disease to people
Do not spread disease to people
questions.explanation: Flies, rats and mosquitoes breed or feed in rubbish and dirty water and can carry germs. Keeping surroundings clean keeps them away.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Match each picture to the healthy need it shows.
questions.explanation: A healthy body needs clean surroundings, safe water, hygiene, nutritious food, exercise and sleep.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: After heavy rain, which object left in the yard could collect still water where mosquitoes lay eggs?
questions.explanation: Aedes mosquitoes lay eggs in small amounts of still water, in containers such as buckets, old tyres and flower tubs. Emptying them every week breaks the life cycle.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Which picture shows a symptom, a sign that a person is ill?
questions.explanation: A fever is a symptom of illness. The thermometer shows the child's temperature is high.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Which pictures show things a healthy body needs? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Healthy bodies need nutritious food, exercise and sleep. Hours of television and sugary sweets do not build a healthy lifestyle.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Germs are too small to see with our eyes alone. Which tool do scientists use to see them?
questions.explanation: A microscope makes tiny things look much bigger. A telescope is for faraway objects and a thermometer measures temperature.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: The tubewell near Tuli's home is broken, and the only water is from a pond. What is the best way to make it safer to drink?
options: Add a spoonful of sugar.
Let it stand for an hour.
Put it in a fridge.
Boil it before drinking.
questions.explanation: Boiling kills the germs that cause diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid. Filtering and using a safe tubewell also work. Sugar, standing or chilling do not remove germs.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Rafi's family keeps flower tubs of rainwater on the roof. During the monsoon, what should they do to lower the risk of dengue?
options: Leave them, because mosquitoes breed only in dirty water.
Cover them only at night.
Empty and scrub the tubs at least once a week.
Fill the tubs to the top so they never dry out.
questions.explanation: Aedes mosquitoes lay eggs in clean, still water, and the young need about 7 to 10 days to become adults. Emptying and scrubbing weekly stops them. These mosquitoes bite in the daytime.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Class 5 is making rules to keep their school healthy. Which are good rules? Choose all that are right.
options: Wash hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet.
Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or your elbow.
Share one cup and one water bottle with friends.
Put rubbish in the bin.
Throw wrappers on the playground.
questions.explanation: Handwashing, covering coughs and putting rubbish in bins all stop germs from spreading. Sharing cups spreads germs and loose rubbish attracts flies and rats.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Example data: a city hospital had 52 dengue patients in July and 214 in September. There were ___ more patients in September than in July.
questions.explanation: 214 − 52 = 162. Dengue cases rise during and after the monsoon, when rain leaves water in containers where mosquitoes breed.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Nadia spends every afternoon watching television and eating crisps. Her mother wants to help her stay healthy. Which advice is best?
options: Play for about an hour a day and eat more fruit.
Drink more sugary drinks every afternoon to get energy.
Sleep less each night so there is more time.
Stay indoors all day to keep away from germs.
questions.explanation: Children need about an hour of activity each day and a balanced diet. Too little exercise and too much sugar and fat are linked to diseases such as diabetes and heart disease.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Explain why a city with good drains, clean water and toilets has fewer cases of diarrhoea.
questions.model_answer: Diarrhoea germs spread through dirty water and human waste. Good drains and toilets keep waste away from drinking water and food, and clean water has no germs, so fewer people get ill.
questions.explanation: Clean surroundings and safe water cut the route by which germs travel from waste to people's mouths. Prevention works by breaking the chain of infection.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Example class experiment: pupils rubbed glitter (a model of germs) onto their hands and washed. The mean number of glitter pieces left was 58 for water only, 27 for soap for 5 seconds and 5 for soap for 20 seconds. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Water alone is enough to remove all the germs from hands.
Soap for 20 seconds removed the most glitter ("germs").
Soap for 5 seconds works as well as soap for 20 seconds.
The glitter model proves that soap kills all the germs.
questions.explanation: The fewest pieces (5) were left after 20 seconds with soap. The experiment shows how much glitter is removed, not whether anything is killed, so the last statement goes beyond the evidence.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: In the glitter experiment, which is a limitation of using glitter as a model for germs?
options: Glitter sticks to hands and spreads to things we touch.
Glitter can be washed off hands with water and soap.
Glitter pieces can be counted to give a number.
Glitter is much bigger than germs and is not alive.
questions.explanation: A model is useful but never exactly like the real thing. Real germs are far too small to see and can multiply, but glitter is large, visible and not alive.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: Example data: dengue patients at a city hospital were Jan 12, Mar 18, May 45, Jul 240, Sep 360 and Nov 130. Which statements are supported by the data? Choose all that are right.
options: The most patients came in September.
There were 315 more patients in September than in May.
The number of patients fell between January and May.
The fewest patients came in July.
Mosquitoes breed only in winter.
questions.explanation: September has the highest number (360), and 360 − 45 = 315. The numbers rose from January to May, July was high not low, and the data say nothing about winter breeding.

questions.title: Staying Healthy
questions.stem: In a village, 9 out of every 10 children are vaccinated against measles. Why is a measles outbreak less likely to spread there?
options: The measles germs die as soon as they reach the air.
Vaccines kill measles germs on the skin of children.
Most children cannot catch it, so the germ spreads less.
Unvaccinated children can never catch measles from anyone.
questions.explanation: When most people are protected, the germ has few people to spread to. This also helps protect babies and sick children who cannot be vaccinated.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Match each nutrient to its job in the body.
pairs: helps food move through the gut
questions.explanation: Each nutrient has its own job, so we need a variety of foods. Iodine comes from iodised salt, calcium from milk and small fish, and iron from leafy greens, meat and eggs.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Sort each food by the main nutrient it gives.
questions.explanation: Starchy foods give energy, foods such as fish, eggs and dal help us grow and repair, and fruit and vegetables keep the body healthy with vitamins and minerals.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: A balanced diet means eating a ___ of foods in the right ___.
questions.explanation: No single food has every nutrient, so we need a variety of foods. Eating too little or too much of any food is not balanced.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: A healthy plate is half vegetables and fruit, a quarter ___ (such as rice or roti) and a quarter ___ (such as fish, egg or dal).
questions.explanation: The guidelines say not to fill the plate with rice alone. Half of the plate should be vegetables and fruit, with smaller shares of grains and protein.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to find out how much sugar a drink contains and whether it is a good choice.
sequence: Find the grams of sugar in one serving on the label.
Divide the grams by 4, because 4 g make 1 teaspoon.
Write down the number of teaspoons.
Compare it with the daily limit of about 6 teaspoons.
Decide whether the drink is a good choice.
questions.explanation: Reading a label, converting grams to teaspoons and comparing with a limit turns a number into advice you can act on.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: The body needs some fat for energy and warmth, so we should never eat any fat.
questions.explanation: The statement contradicts itself. We need a little fat, for example from oil, nuts or fish, but too much fried and fatty food is unhealthy. Moderation means not too much and not too little.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Which pieces of advice follow the dietary guidelines for Bangladesh? Choose all that are right.
options: Eat a variety of foods every day.
Fill the plate with rice alone.
Eat plenty of vegetables and fruit.
Use iodised salt.
Eat fried snacks every day.
questions.explanation: The guidelines advise variety, plenty of vegetables and fruit and iodised salt, and to limit salt, sugar, oil and fried snacks.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Match each example to the factor that affects food choices.
pairs: Fresh vegetables cost more than packets of snacks.
Mangoes are plentiful only in summer.
Families eat semai at Eid and pitha in winter.
Adverts and food-delivery apps make fast food look exciting.
questions.explanation: People's food choices depend on cost, what is available, family and cultural traditions, and the influence of media and technology.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Which food is a good source of iron, which helps blood carry oxygen?
options: lal shak (red spinach)
white sugar
cooking oil
cola
questions.explanation: Leafy greens such as lal shak, as well as meat and eggs, give iron. Sugar, oil and cola give energy but almost no iron.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Why should children avoid tea, cola and energy drinks in the evening?
options: They contain too much protein for the body to use.
They make the bones soft if drunk at night.
Caffeine in them can stop children sleeping well.
They stop the stomach from digesting food.
questions.explanation: Tea, coffee, cola and energy drinks contain caffeine, which keeps the brain awake. Children need plenty of sleep to grow and learn.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Imran's lunch is a big plate of white rice with a little dal, and a glass of cola. Explain why this is not a balanced meal.
questions.model_answer: It is mostly carbohydrate from rice and has little protein. It has no vegetables or fruit for vitamins, minerals and fibre, and cola is full of sugar. A balanced meal needs a variety of foods in the right amounts.
questions.explanation: A balanced meal has a variety of foods in the right proportions: about half vegetables and fruit, a quarter grains and a quarter protein, with water rather than a sugary drink.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Which food is the best source of protein?
questions.explanation: Eggs, like fish, meat, dal and milk, give protein for growth and repair. Rice gives mainly energy, and lollipops and chips give sugar or fat.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Sort the foods into everyday foods and occasional treats.
questions.explanation: Fruit, vegetables, fish and rice can be part of daily meals. Sugary and fried foods are fine now and then, but the guidelines say to limit sugar, oil and fried snacks.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Which drink contains caffeine?
questions.explanation: Caffeine is found in tea, coffee, cola and energy drinks. It can keep children awake at night.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Match each food picture to the nutrient it helps to give.
questions.explanation: Different foods give different nutrients. Milk and small fish give calcium, leafy greens give iron, iodised salt gives iodine and rice gives carbohydrate.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Which pictures show foods with a lot of added sugar? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Sweets, doughnuts and ice cream contain a lot of added sugar, which can cause tooth decay and, if eaten too often, obesity. Carrots and rice have no added sugar.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Which of these is a drug that children should take only when a doctor or parent gives it?
questions.explanation: Medicines are drugs. They help when used correctly, but the wrong medicine or too much can harm the body, so only take them as a doctor or parent says.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Rafi has 60 taka for school tiffin. Prices: banana 10, boiled egg 15, roti (2 pieces) 10, vegetable bhaji 20, guava 15, chips 20, cola 35, water 15. Which tiffin is balanced and costs no more than 60 taka?
options: chips, boiled egg, banana and cola, total 80 Tk
roti, bhaji, egg and banana, total 55 Tk
cola, guava, vegetable bhaji and water, total 85 Tk
chips and cola, total 55 Tk
questions.explanation: Roti (carbohydrate), egg (protein), bhaji and banana (vitamins and fibre) cost 10 + 20 + 15 + 10 = 55 Tk. Chips and cola fit the budget but are mostly fat and sugar. The other tiffins cost too much.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Imran's family lives in a city. They buy instant noodles more often than fresh vegetables. Which is the most likely reason?
options: Vegetables are not sold anywhere in the city.
Noodles contain more vitamins than vegetables.
Noodles are cheap and quick to cook.
Doctors say noodles are the healthiest food.
questions.explanation: Cost and convenience strongly affect food choices, along with adverts and taste. Noodles are not richer in vitamins, but a busy family may find them quicker and cheaper.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Raju's older cousin offers him a cigarette and says, "Just try it once." What is the best thing for Raju to do?
options: Try a little, because one cigarette cannot do any harm to him.
Take it, but only smoke it when his parents are away from home.
Accept it politely so that his cousin does not laugh at him.
Say no, because tobacco harms the lungs and heart.
questions.explanation: Tobacco harms the mouth, lungs and heart and is very hard to stop using. The safest choice is not to start, and Raju can talk to a trusted adult.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Example label: a 250 ml mango juice drink has 32 g of sugar. Since 4 g make 1 teaspoon, it contains ___ teaspoons of sugar.
questions.explanation: 32 ÷ 4 = 8 teaspoons of sugar in one small serving. That is more than the whole day's limit of about 6 teaspoons for children.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Moung finds some pills on the road. His friend says they are vitamins, so it is safe to take one.
questions.explanation: Never take pills you have found or that nobody trusted has given you. Unknown pills could be dangerous drugs. Moung should give them to a teacher or parent.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Nadia's school canteen sells mostly chips, sweets and cola. Suggest two changes the canteen could make, and explain how they would help learners.
questions.model_answer: The canteen could sell fruit, boiled eggs and water instead of chips and cola. This gives learners vitamins, protein and less sugar, so they stay healthier and have less tooth decay and obesity.
questions.explanation: Offering fruit, water, eggs and vegetables while selling fewer sugary and fried snacks makes the healthy choice the easy choice. It helps prevent obesity, tooth decay and later diseases such as diabetes.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: In the simulation, the person eats a lot of food but does very little exercise. What happens to their weight over time?

sim.task: Open Eating and Exercise. Choose plenty of food for the person's diet and only a little activity or exercise. Run the simulation and watch the energy in, the energy used and the person's weight over time.

options: Weight goes down, because less energy goes in than is used.
Weight goes up, because more energy goes in than is used.
Weight stays the same, because food does not matter.
Weight goes down, because exercise makes more energy.
questions.explanation: When more energy comes in from food than the body uses, the extra is stored and weight goes up over time. This is why moderation in food and enough exercise both matter.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: In the simulation, when you add more exercise and keep the same food, the energy used goes up.

sim.task: Open Eating and Exercise. Choose a diet and look at the energy used. Then add more daily activity or exercise without changing the food, and look at the energy used again.

questions.explanation: Activity uses energy, so more exercise means more energy used each day. If the food stays the same, there is less left over to be stored.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: You find a diet and exercise plan that keeps the person's weight steady. What is true about the energy in from food and the energy used?

sim.task: Open Eating and Exercise. Try different foods and different amounts of activity until the person's weight stays steady over time. Compare the energy in from food with the energy used.

options: Energy in is much bigger than energy used.
Energy used is much bigger than energy in.
Energy in is zero.
They are about equal.
questions.explanation: Weight stays steady when the energy in from food is about equal to the energy used. More in than out makes weight go up, and less in than out makes it go down.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Example label: a 250 ml drink has 28 g of sugar. Children should have no more than about 24 g (6 teaspoons) a day. The drink holds ___ teaspoons of sugar (4 g = 1 teaspoon), so one serving is ___ g over the daily limit.
questions.explanation: 28 ÷ 4 = 7 teaspoons. The limit is 24 g, and 28 − 24 = 4 g, which is 1 teaspoon over. One small drink uses up more than the whole day's sugar.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Raju has 50 taka. Prices: banana 10, boiled egg 15, roti (2 pieces) 10, vegetable bhaji 20, guava 15, chips 20, cola 35, water 15. Which tiffin is balanced and costs no more than 50 taka?
options: roti, bhaji, egg and water, total 60 Tk
chips, cola and banana, total 65 Tk
roti, boiled egg and guava, total 40 Tk
banana and guava only, total 25 Tk
questions.explanation: Roti gives carbohydrate, egg gives protein and guava gives vitamins, for 10 + 15 + 15 = 40 Tk. Banana and guava alone fit the budget but have no carbohydrate or protein. The other two cost more than 50 Tk.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Which statements are true? Choose all that are right.
options: Eating too little food can stop children growing properly.
Healthy food eaten in huge amounts is always good for you.
Too much sugary and fatty food can lead to obesity and, later, diabetes.
Caffeine can stop children sleeping well.
Fat should never be eaten.
questions.explanation: Both too little and too much food cause problems, so moderation matters. Even healthy food can be eaten in the wrong amounts, and a little fat is needed for energy and warmth.

questions.title: Eating for Health
questions.stem: Fifty years ago many Bangladeshi children were too short because of undernutrition. Today doctors in towns see more overweight children. What is the best explanation?
options: More people buy fast food, fried snacks and sugary drinks, and children are less active.
Children now eat far too many vegetables.
There is less food grown in the country now.
Drinking water makes children overweight.
questions.explanation: The country grows more food now, so fewer children are undernourished. But in towns more fast food, fried snacks, sugary drinks and screen time cause overnutrition for some.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: What is the job of the food store inside a seed?
options: It gives the embryo its energy.
It catches light energy for the seed to use.
It protects the seed from damage and drying out.
It takes in water from the soil for the seed.
questions.explanation: The embryo has no leaves yet, so it cannot make food. The food store gives it energy until the leaves grow. The seed coat is the part that protects the seed.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Match each plant part to its job.
pairs: take in water and hold the plant in the soil
holds the plant up and carries water
use light energy to make food
questions.explanation: Each part of a plant has a job. Leaves make food, roots and stem look after water and support, and flowers make seeds.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Does each sentence describe a seed before germination, or a plant with leaves?
items: gets its energy from a food store
is protected by a tough seed coat
makes its own food in its leaves
has chlorophyll to trap light energy
questions.explanation: A seed has no leaves, so it lives on its food store. Once leaves open, the plant makes its own food using light energy trapped by chlorophyll.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Put the stages of germination in order.
sequence: The seed absorbs water and swells.
The seed coat splits.
The first root grows down into the soil.
The first shoot grows up towards the light.
The first leaves open and the seed shrivels.
questions.explanation: Water starts germination. The root grows first to take in water and hold the plant, then the shoot grows up and the leaves open. The food store is used up, so the seed shrivels.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Seeds need water, warmth and ___ to germinate, but they do not need ___.
questions.explanation: Seeds can germinate deep in dark soil because their food store gives them energy. Light matters later, once the plant has leaves.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Seeds need light to germinate.
questions.explanation: Seeds do not need light to germinate because the food store gives them energy. That is why seeds can germinate deep in dark soil.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: A plant kept in the dark grows tall, thin and pale.
questions.explanation: Without light the plant cannot make food. It stretches upwards, its leaves turn pale yellow and in the end it dies.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Which green substance in leaves traps light energy?
options: nutrients
chlorophyll
the embryo
the food store
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll traps light energy so that the leaf can make food. Nutrients are minerals taken in from the soil.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: A plant with leaves needs certain things to grow well. Which are they? Choose all that are right.
options: light
water
warmth
air
a seed coat
questions.explanation: Plants need light, water, warmth and air. A seed coat protects a seed but a grown plant does not need one.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Why does a seed need a food store, but a grown plant does not?
questions.model_answer: A seed has no leaves yet, so it cannot make food. The food store gives it energy until its leaves grow and make food using light.
questions.explanation: The seed lives on stored food until the first leaves open. A grown plant makes food in its leaves using light energy.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Where do plants make their food?
options: in their roots and stem
in the soil around them
in their leaves
in their seeds and fruits
questions.explanation: Plants make food in their leaves, using light energy. The roots take in water and nutrients from the soil, but the soil is not their food.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Roots take in water and ___ from the soil, and they hold the plant in place.
questions.explanation: Roots absorb water and nutrients (minerals), which help the plant stay healthy. They also anchor the plant in the ground.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: What happens to the seed's food store as the seedling grows leaves?
options: It grows bigger and bigger each day.
It turns into the tough seed coat.
It changes into the green chlorophyll.
It is used up and the seed shrivels.
questions.explanation: The seedling uses the stored food for energy. When the leaves open and start making food, the empty seed shrivels away.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Match each key word to its meaning.
pairs: when a seed starts to grow
the tiny plant inside a seed
to take in, like a sponge takes in water
green substance that traps light energy
minerals from the soil that help plants stay healthy
questions.explanation: These key words describe how a seed turns into a plant and how a plant gets what it needs.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Look at the tall, thin, pale plant. Which factor is it missing?
questions.image_alt: Four potted plants: a healthy plant, a wilted plant with no water, a tall pale plant with no light and a very small plant that is too cold.
options: water
warmth
air
light
questions.explanation: A plant without light cannot make food. It grows tall and thin, with pale leaves, as it stretches to look for light.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Look at the very small plant that has hardly grown. Which factor is it missing?
questions.image_alt: Four potted plants: a healthy plant, a wilted plant with no water, a tall pale plant with no light and a very small plant that is too cold.
options: water
light
warmth
a food store
questions.explanation: A plant that is too cold grows very slowly, so it stays small. A plant without water would droop, and one without light would be tall and pale.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Which numbers show parts of the embryo? Choose all that are right.
questions.image_alt: Inside a bean seed with parts numbered: 1 seed coat, 2 scar, 3 food store, 4 embryo root, 5 embryo shoot.
questions.explanation: The embryo is the tiny baby plant: its first root (4) and first shoot (5). The seed coat (1) protects it, and the food store (3) feeds it.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Which number shows the part that uses light energy to make food?
questions.image_alt: A plant with five parts numbered: 1 flower, 2 leaf, 3 stem, 4 roots, 5 fruit.
questions.explanation: Leaves (2) make food using light energy. Roots (4) take in water, the stem (3) carries it, and the flower (1) makes seeds.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: A white flower stands in coloured water, and the colour travels up to the petals. What does this show?
questions.image_alt: A white flower stem in coloured water with the colour travelling up the stem to the petals.
options: Water moves up the stem.
Water moves down the roots.
The petals make coloured water.
The flower makes its own food.
questions.explanation: The coloured water is carried up the stem to the flower. The stem holds the plant up and carries water around it.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: The plant with drooping, wilted leaves is the one that has no water.
questions.image_alt: Four potted plants: a healthy plant, a wilted plant with no water, a tall pale plant with no light and a very small plant that is too cold.
questions.explanation: Plants droop when they do not get enough water. Without water the stem and leaves lose their firmness.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: A farmer plants rice seeds in a field covered by flood water. Few seeds germinate. Why?
options: The flood water blocks light that the seeds need.
They cannot get enough air under the flood water.
Flood water is far too bright for seeds.
The seeds need dry soil to absorb water.
questions.explanation: Seeds need air (oxygen) as well as water to germinate. Under deep flood water they cannot get enough air and may rot. Seeds do not need light to germinate.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Rice farmers in Bangladesh first grow seeds in a small, wet seedbed. Why is the wet soil important?
options: The seeds need to stay in the dark.
The seeds need the Sun to be hot.
The seeds need less air.
The seeds need water to germinate.
questions.explanation: Germination begins when a seed absorbs water and swells. A warm, wet seedbed gives the seeds what they need.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Mina keeps a pot plant in a dark cupboard and waters it every day. She says it will grow well because it gets water. Is she right?
questions.explanation: A plant with leaves also needs light to make food. In the dark cupboard it will grow tall, thin and pale, even with water.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: The pot plant on Imran's windowsill leans towards the window. Why?
options: Plants grow away from the wall.
Plants lean to find water.
Plants grow towards the light.
The window is warmer than the room.
questions.explanation: Leaves need light to make food, so plants grow towards the light. Turning the pot makes the plant grow upright again.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: In southern Bangladesh, farmers grow vegetables on floating gardens made of water hyacinth. Why is this a clever idea?
questions.model_answer: It turns a problem weed into compost and a raft for growing food, and it helps clear the rivers.
questions.explanation: The rotting water hyacinth makes rich compost full of nutrients, and the garden rises and falls with the flood water, so the crops never drown.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Class 5A put 20 cress seeds in each dish. Dish 1: warm, wet, in the light. Dish 2: warm, wet, in the dark. Dish 3: cold, wet, in the dark. Dish 4: warm, dry, in the light. Which two dishes should they compare to find out if seeds need warmth?
options: Dish 1 and Dish 2
Dish 2 and Dish 3
Dish 1 and Dish 4
Dish 3 and Dish 4
questions.explanation: Dishes 2 and 3 differ in only one thing: temperature. Dishes 1 and 2 test light, and Dishes 1 and 4 test water. Dishes 3 and 4 differ in several ways, so they would not be a fair comparison.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Nadia and Tanvir counted leaves each week. In week 4 Plant A (in the light) had 12 leaves and Plant B (in the dark) had 5 leaves. Plant A had ___ more leaves than Plant B.
questions.explanation: 12 - 5 = 7. These results are an example from a class investigation into light and plant growth.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Plant B (in the dark cupboard) went from 5 leaves in week 4 to 4 leaves in week 5. What is the best explanation?
options: Without light it could not make food.
The plant grew a new leaf and lost two.
Plants in the dark need a lot more water.
The seed's food store had been used up.
questions.explanation: A plant with leaves needs light to make food. In the dark it weakens, its leaves turn yellow and some fall off. The food store belongs to the seed, which is long gone.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: A seed is planted deep in dark soil. Will it germinate? Explain your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, if it has water, warmth and air. Seeds do not need light to germinate because they use their food store for energy.
questions.explanation: Germination needs water, warmth and air. The seed's food store gives it energy, so it does not need light until the leaves open.

questions.title: Plants: Seeds, Germination and Growth
questions.stem: Nadia tests whether the amount of water changes how tall bean plants grow. Which things should she keep the same? Choose all that are right.
options: the type of bean
the size of the pot
the amount of light
the amount of water
the temperature
questions.explanation: In a fair test only one thing changes: the amount of water. Everything else, such as bean, pot, light and temperature, must stay the same.

questions.title: Flowering Plants: Reproduction and Life Cycles
questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: pollen moves from an anther to a stigma
a male cell joins with a female cell in an ovule
seeds are carried away from the parent plant
a sweet liquid that attracts insects
a powder made by the anther
questions.explanation: Pollination comes first, then fertilisation makes a seed. Dispersal spreads the seeds and germination starts a new plant.

questions.title: Flowering Plants: Reproduction and Life Cycles
questions.stem: Sort the flower parts into male, female and other parts.
questions.explanation: The stamen (anther and filament) is the male part. The carpel (stigma, style, ovary with ovules) is the female part. Petals and sepals attract insects and protect the bud.

questions.title: Flowering Plants: Reproduction and Life Cycles
questions.stem: After a bee visits a flower, what happens? Put the steps in order.
sequence: A bee carries pollen from another flower.
Pollen lands on the sticky stigma.
A pollen tube grows down the style to the ovary.
The male cell joins the female cell in the ovule.
The ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit.
The fruit is eaten and the seed is dropped far away.
questions.explanation: Pollination comes first, then the pollen tube carries the male cell to the ovule for fertilisation. The seed and fruit form, and dispersal spreads the seed.

questions.title: Flowering Plants: Reproduction and Life Cycles
questions.stem: The anther is a female part of the flower.
questions.explanation: The anther is part of the stamen, the male part. It makes pollen. The female part is the carpel, with the stigma, style and ovary.

questions.title: Flowering Plants: Reproduction and Life Cycles
questions.stem: Wind-pollinated flowers usually have big, bright petals and a sweet smell.
questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers, such as grasses and maize, are small and dull with no scent or nectar. They do not need to attract insects.

questions.title: Flowering Plants: Reproduction and Life Cycles
questions.stem: Pollen is made in the ___, and it is caught by the sticky ___.
questions.explanation: Pollen forms in the anther. For pollination, it must travel to the sticky stigma at the top of the carpel.

questions.title: Flowering Plants: Reproduction and Life Cycles
questions.stem: After fertilisation, each fertilised ovule becomes a ___ and the ovary grows into a ___.
questions.explanation: The seed holds the baby plant, and the fruit protects the seeds. A mango has one large seed, but a tomato has many.

questions.title: Flowering Plants: Reproduction and Life Cycles
questions.stem: Which part of a flower becomes the fruit?
options: the petal
the stigma
the ovary
the anther
questions.explanation: After fertilisation the petals wither and fall, and the ovary grows into the fruit that protects the seeds.

questions.title: Flowering Plants: Reproduction and Life Cycles
