questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Match each 'R' to an example.
pairs: say no to a plastic straw
turn off the tap while brushing teeth
turn old paper into new paper
questions.explanation: Refuse and reduce stop waste before it starts. Reuse keeps things in use, recycling makes new products from old materials, and rotting turns food and plant waste into compost.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Coal, oil and gas are called ___ fuels because they formed from ancient living things. Using resources without harming future generations is called ___ use.
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from ancient plants and animals. Sustainable use meets our needs today without stopping future people from meeting theirs.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Bangladesh makes most of its electricity from natural gas, a non-renewable resource.
questions.explanation: Natural gas is a fossil fuel. The gas fields in Bangladesh are slowly running out, so millions of homes now use solar panels and more solar parks are being built.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: A renewable resource can never run out, however much of it we use.
questions.explanation: Only some, such as sunlight and wind, never run out. Trees and fish are renewable, but they can run out if we take them faster than they regenerate.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which of these harm the Earth's resources? Choose all that are right.
options: catching too many fish, including young ones
cutting down forests faster than they regrow
planting a new tree for each tree cut
dumping plastic into rivers
protecting young hilsa so they can grow
questions.explanation: Over-fishing, over-cutting and dumping plastic all damage resources. Planting trees and protecting young fish help the resources regenerate.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Why is natural gas called non-renewable, even though it was made by nature?
questions.model_answer: It took millions of years to form from ancient living things, and we are using it much faster than it can form again.
questions.explanation: Natural gas forms very slowly, over millions of years. People use it up far faster than nature can make more, so once it is gone it is gone for us.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which phrase best describes sustainable use of resources?
options: using as much as we can while it is still cheap to buy
never using any natural resource at all
using only the resources that cost nothing
meeting our needs without harming future people
questions.explanation: Sustainable use means we can meet our needs today and people in the future can still meet theirs.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Trees are renewable, yet some forests disappear. Which is the best explanation?
options: Renewable resources are never changed by anything people do.
Trees stop growing once they are about ten years old.
People cut trees faster than the forest can grow back.
Forests are made of non-renewable materials.
questions.explanation: A forest can take 20 to 50 years or more to regrow. If trees are cut faster than they grow back, the forest shrinks, so even renewable resources can run out.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Planting a new tree for every tree that is cut down is a sustainable way to use a forest.
questions.explanation: The forest regrows about as fast as it is used, so there will still be trees for future generations. This is sustainable.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which picture shows an energy source that will never run out?
questions.explanation: Wind never runs out, so it is renewable. Cars and factories mostly burn fossil fuels, which take millions of years to form.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Match each picture to the 'R' it shows.
pairs: reuse: use it again and again
recycle: make it into a new product
rot: compost food and plant waste
refuse: say no to what you do not need
questions.explanation: The 5 Rs are refuse, reduce, reuse, recycle and rot. Each one helps to save resources and cut down waste.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Which picture shows a renewable resource that can still run out if people take too much?
questions.explanation: Fish are renewable because they breed, but if too many adults and young fish are caught, the numbers fall. Sunlight and wind cannot be used up.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Dhaka banned thin plastic bags in 2002 because they blocked drains. Which picture shows a better choice for carrying shopping?
questions.explanation: A reusable bag can be used again and again, so it replaces many thin plastic bags. This is the 'reuse' and 'refuse' idea.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into actions that help the Earth and actions that harm it.
questions.explanation: Planting trees, recycling and using solar energy protect resources. Oil spills and smoke from burning fuels pollute the land, water and air.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: At a river market, a seller offers Nadia a basket of tiny jatka (young hilsa) cheaply. What is the best choice for the future of the hilsa?
options: Buy them, because small fish taste the sweetest.
Buy them, because the fish have already been caught anyway.
Do not buy them: they need time to grow and breed.
Buy them, because hilsa will always come back.
questions.explanation: Jatka are young fish that have not yet bred. Catching them is banned for several months so that they can grow up and lay eggs, which keeps the hilsa population renewable.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Class 5A found that most of their week's rubbish was paper and food waste. Which plan would cut the most waste?
options: Ask everyone to bring more new paper each week.
Buy more plastic wrappers to keep the snacks fresh and clean.
Put the paper and the food waste in the same bin.
Use both sides of the paper and compost the food waste.
questions.explanation: Using both sides of paper is 'reduce', and composting food waste is 'rot'. Both turn waste into something useful or stop it being made.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Tuli wants to save resources at home. Which actions would help? Choose all that are right.
options: Turn off fans and lights when leaving a room.
Fix a dripping tap.
Leave the tap running while brushing teeth.
Carry water in a reusable bottle.
Throw all food waste into the drain.
questions.explanation: Saving electricity, mending leaks and reusing a bottle all reduce waste. A running tap wastes water, and food waste in the drain blocks it, when it could be composted.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: The gas fields in Bangladesh are slowly running out. Which choice is best for the future?
options: Use up the remaining gas as fast as we possibly can.
Stop making any electricity in the country.
Build more solar parks and solar roofs.
Install diesel generators in every village and city.
questions.explanation: Sunlight is renewable and never runs out, so solar power can meet our needs now without taking away the needs of future generations. Gas and diesel are non-renewable.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Banning thin plastic bags in 2002 helped Dhaka, because the bags had been blocking drains and making floods worse.
questions.explanation: Bangladesh was one of the first countries to ban thin plastic bags. Fewer bags in the drains means less flooding, and less plastic in rivers and soil harms fewer animals.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: What happens to the temperature when you add more greenhouse gases?

sim.task: Open Greenhouse Effect. Find the control for the amount of greenhouse gases. Make the amount bigger and watch the thermometer and the heat that goes back up from the Earth.

options: It goes up because more heat is trapped.
It goes down because more heat escapes.
It stays the same whatever the gases do.
It drops to zero straight away.
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases trap heat that would otherwise escape, so the temperature rises. Burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas adds greenhouse gases to the air.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: When you reduce the amount of greenhouse gases, less heat is trapped and the temperature goes down.

sim.task: Open Greenhouse Effect. Use the control for the amount of greenhouse gases to make the amount smaller. Watch the thermometer.

questions.explanation: With fewer greenhouse gases, more heat escapes back into space, so the temperature falls. Using less fuel is one way people can help.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: In one week Class 5A collected rubbish (in grams): paper and card 1800, plastic 950, food waste 1200, pencil shavings 150, other 300. The total is ___ g. Food waste and pencil shavings, which can be composted, make ___ g.
questions.explanation: 1800 + 950 + 1200 + 150 + 300 = 4400 g. Compostable waste is 1200 + 150 = 1350 g, so about three tenths of the rubbish could rot into compost.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: The hilsa catch in Bangladesh was about 3.0 lakh tonnes in 2008–09 and about 5.7 lakh tonnes in 2020–21 (1 lakh = 100 000). About how many more tonnes were caught in 2020–21?
options: 2.7 tonnes
27 000 tonnes
270 000 tonnes
2 700 000 tonnes
questions.explanation: 5.7 − 3.0 = 2.7 lakh tonnes, and 2.7 × 100 000 = 270 000 tonnes. The catch rose because the fishing bans let more fish breed and grow.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Sumi says, 'Bamboo is renewable, so we can cut as much as we like.' What is wrong with her idea?
options: Bamboo is non-renewable, so it can never regrow.
It can still run out if we cut it faster than it regrows.
Bamboo takes millions of years to grow back again.
Nothing is wrong, since renewable always means unlimited.
questions.explanation: Bamboo regrows in 3 to 5 years, so it is renewable. But if we cut it faster than it regrows, we will run out. Renewable does not mean unlimited.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Fishing for hilsa is banned for several months of the year and for 22 days in the main breeding season. Explain how this helps both the fish and the fishing families in the future.
questions.model_answer: The bans let adult hilsa breed and the young fish grow up, so the population grows back. Then fishers can keep catching fish in the future.
questions.explanation: Hilsa are renewable only if enough are left to breed. The bans give them time to regenerate, so the catch rises and families can keep fishing.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: A woodcutter cuts 10 mahogany trees each year (example). Each tree needs about 50 years to grow back. How many trees must the forest have so that this can go on for ever?
options: 500 trees
60 trees
100 trees
5 trees
questions.explanation: In 50 years the woodcutter cuts 10 × 50 = 500 trees. With 500 trees, the first trees cut have regrown by the time the last are cut, so the cutting is sustainable.

questions.title: Resources and Sustainability
questions.stem: Approximate hilsa catch in lakh tonnes: 2008–09: 3.0, 2012–13: 3.5, 2016–17: 5.0, 2020–21: 5.7. Which statements are supported by the data? Choose all that are right.
options: The catch rose in every period shown.
The catch almost doubled between 2008–09 and 2020–21.
The bans are the only possible cause of the rise.
The biggest rise was between 2012–13 and 2016–17.
The catch in 2016–17 was 50 000 tonnes.
questions.explanation: The rises were 0.5, 1.5 and 0.7 lakh tonnes, and 5.7 is almost twice 3.0. The data cannot show that bans are the only cause, and 5.0 lakh tonnes is 500 000 tonnes, not 50 000.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: A **system** is…
options: a single machine that has only one moving part
a simple drawing that shows something real
a set of parts that work together and affect each other
a tool that people made long ago
questions.explanation: A system has parts, connections between them, and often inputs and outputs. A bicycle, a beehive and the water cycle are all systems.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: A good model always shows everything about the real thing.
questions.explanation: Every model leaves some things out. A globe shows the shape of the Earth but not its real size or the moving clouds.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Match each technology to the civilisation it came from.
questions.explanation: Mohenjo-daro in the Indus Valley had covered drains, Egyptians used the shadoof, Persians built windcatchers and qanats, China gave us the compass and paper, and Bengal weavers made muslin.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: A model is a simpler way of showing something real, but every model has ___.
questions.explanation: A limitation is something a model cannot show. Good scientists always ask what a model shows well and what it leaves out.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: A hand tube-well is a system. Sort these into input, part or output.
questions.explanation: The input is what goes in (your push). The parts work together inside the pump. The output is what comes out (water).

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Which of these are systems? Choose all that are right.
options: a bicycle
a single loose stone
a beehive
the water cycle
a blank sheet of paper
questions.explanation: A bicycle, a beehive and the water cycle each have several parts that work together. A single stone or one sheet of paper has no connected parts.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a windcatcher cools a house.
sequence: Wind blows against the tall tower.
The tower catches the breeze.
The air is sent down into the house.
Cooler moving air flows through the rooms.
questions.explanation: A windcatcher uses only the wind. It catches the breeze and sends it down, so no electricity is needed.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Sort these into a model or the real thing.
items: a cycle rickshaw you can ride
questions.explanation: A model is a simpler stand-in for something real. A globe stands for the Earth, a map stands for a town and a toy stands for a real vehicle.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: A shadoof is a kind of lever.
questions.explanation: The shadoof is a long pole on a pivot with a bucket at one end and a heavy weight at the other. Ancient Egyptians used it to lift water from the Nile.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Covered drains in Mohenjo-daro helped to stop diseases from spreading.
questions.explanation: The drains carried dirty water and waste away from homes, so fewer germs spread. Today’s sewers follow the same idea.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Explain how a shadoof makes lifting water easier.
questions.model_answer: It is a lever on a pivot. The heavy weight on one end helps to lift the full bucket, so the farmer needs less force.
questions.explanation: The counterweight does part of the lifting work, so the person needs to push less hard to raise the bucket.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: What goes into a system is the ___, and what comes out is the ___.
questions.explanation: The input is what goes in, such as your push on a tube-well handle. The output is what comes out, such as the water.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Match each model to something it does **not** show.
pairs: the real amount of water in the seas
questions.explanation: No model shows everything. Knowing what a model leaves out tells us how far we can trust it.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: This tube-well is a system. Which part do you push on to give the **input**?
questions.image_alt: A hand tubewell with parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Number 1 is the handle (a lever). Your push on the handle is the input that makes the pump work.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Look at the tube-well. Which number is the **output**, where the water comes out?
questions.image_alt: A hand tubewell with parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Number 4 is the spout, where water comes out. Number 5 is the pipe going down to the underground water.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Which of these is a model of the Earth?
questions.explanation: A globe is a smaller, simpler version of the Earth. A compass shows direction, but it is a tool, not a model of the Earth.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: The diagram is a model of a rice-field food chain. If all the frogs disappeared, which animal would lose its food first?
questions.image_alt: Food chain: grass, grasshopper, frog, snake.
options: the grasshopper
the snake
the grass
the frog
questions.explanation: In the chain, the snake eats the frog. In a system, a change to one part affects the parts connected to it. Fewer frogs also means grasshoppers are eaten less.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Forecasters use a computer model of a cyclone. Which part must it show correctly to predict the **strongest winds**?
questions.image_alt: A tropical cyclone from above with parts numbered 1 to 4.
options: number 2, the eye wall
number 3, the rain bands
number 4, the spin arrows
number 1, the eye
questions.explanation: The eye wall (2) has the strongest winds and rain. The eye (1) in the middle is calm.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: On Monday a forecast said a cyclone would reach the coast on Tuesday. On Tuesday morning the new forecast says Wednesday. What is the best reason?
options: New satellite data improved the model
The forecasters made a careless mistake and cannot be trusted
The model can only predict one day ahead at a time
The forecasters guessed at random the first time
questions.explanation: A forecast is a prediction from a model. As new data arrives from satellites, the model is updated and the prediction becomes more accurate.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: After heavy monsoon rain, the lanes of a Dhaka neighbourhood stay flooded because the drains are blocked with rubbish. Which old idea would help most?
options: building new houses closer to the river bank
using a shadoof to lift the flood water to the fields
digging shallow wells in the middle of the lane
covered drains that carry dirty water away
questions.explanation: Covered drains, kept clear, carry water and waste away. This idea is more than 4000 years old and is still the basis of modern sewers.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: A school in Khulna has a hot classroom and no money for air conditioning. Which windcatcher-style idea could help?
options: painting the roof dark so that it holds more heat
shutting every window and door to keep the air in
a tall vent that catches the breeze and sends it down
adding more desks so that the room feels full
questions.explanation: Persian windcatchers cool buildings with moving air and no electricity. Dark roofs and closed windows would make the room hotter.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Mina makes a water cycle model in a plastic bag taped to a window. Which is a limitation of her model?
options: it shows that water can evaporate and condense
it is tiny and leaves out real seas and rivers
it can be watched for several days at school
it needs only water and sunlight to work
questions.explanation: The bag shows evaporation and condensation well, but it is very small and leaves out real seas, rivers and clouds. All models have limits.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Weavers in the Dhaka region stopped making muslin in the 1800s, but today scientists and weavers have made it again. This shows that old skills can be brought back if people record, study and teach them.
questions.explanation: Scientists found the plant, compared its DNA with old muslin samples, and trained weavers. In 2021 they wove new Dhaka muslin.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Bangladeshi scientists wanted to find the right cotton plant for muslin. How did they use evidence?
questions.model_answer: They compared the DNA of plants they found with DNA from old muslin samples in museums to find a match.
questions.explanation: Old muslin kept in museums holds clues. A plant whose DNA matched the old cloth was the right one to grow again.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Class 5B tested three shoe-box houses (all started at 26 °C). After 20 minutes: A (no tower) 34 °C, B (tower facing the fan) 30 °C, C (tower with a wet cloth) 27 °C. By how much did house C warm up?
questions.explanation: C started at 26 °C and ended at 27 °C, so it warmed by 1 °C. House A warmed by 8 °C and B by 4 °C.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: In the shoe-box test, Joy moves house C to 20 cm from the fan, but A and B stay at 50 cm. Why is this a problem?
options: house C will cool down too slowly to be measured
the lamp will be too far away from house C
the thermometer in house C will break
the test is no longer fair, as two things changed
questions.explanation: In a fair test only one thing changes. If distance changes too, we cannot tell whether the tower, the wet cloth or the fan distance caused the difference.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Rafi says, "The test proves that a wet cloth will cool every real house by 7 °C." What is the best reply?
options: He is right, because the numbers were measured with a thermometer
A tiny shoe-box model cannot show everything about real houses
He is right, because house C was the coolest of the three
He is wrong, because a wet cloth always warms things up
questions.explanation: The model is tiny. Real houses are bigger, have people and rooms, and real wind changes. The model suggests an idea but does not prove it for real houses.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Use the shoe-box results (A 34 °C, B 30 °C, C 27 °C). Which conclusions are supported? Choose all that are right.
options: House C stayed the coolest.
The wet cloth made no difference.
The tower cooled better than no tower.
Windcatchers work in every real house.
The wet cloth cooled more than the tower alone.
questions.explanation: C (27) was cooler than B (30), which was cooler than A (34). So the tower helped, and the wet cloth helped further. The data cannot show what happens in every real house.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Put the steps of the windcatcher model investigation in order.
sequence: Build three shoe-box houses: no tower, tower, tower with wet cloth.
Measure the starting temperature of each box (26 °C).
Place each box 50 cm from the fan and lamp.
Wait 20 minutes.
Measure the temperature inside each box.
Compare the results and name the limits of the model.
questions.explanation: A good investigation sets up, measures at the start, keeps conditions equal, waits for a set time, measures again, and then evaluates the model.

questions.title: Systems, Models and Technologies
questions.stem: Muslin spinners often worked in damp morning air. Using what you know about materials, suggest why.
questions.model_answer: Damp air kept the very fine cotton fibres slightly moist and flexible, so the thin threads did not snap.
questions.explanation: Dry cotton fibres are brittle. A little moisture makes the fibres more flexible, so the threads, almost invisible, could be spun without breaking.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Pure water boils at ___ °C and ice melts at ___ °C.
questions.explanation: Water boils at 100 °C. Ice melts at 0 °C, which is also the temperature at which water freezes.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Evaporation can only happen when water is at 100 °C.
questions.explanation: Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid at any temperature. Wet clothes dry on a cool day too, just more slowly. Boiling is the change that happens at 100 °C.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Match each change of state to what happens.
questions.explanation: Melting and freezing are opposites, and so are evaporation and condensation. Heating causes melting and evaporation; cooling causes freezing and condensation.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Match each state of matter to how its particles behave.
pairs: close together, sliding past each other
far apart, moving fast in all directions
questions.explanation: A solid keeps its shape because its particles cannot move away. A liquid flows because its particles slide past each other. A gas spreads out because its particles are far apart and move quickly.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Each change needs heat to be added or heat to be removed. Sort them.
items: a puddle drying up in the sun
dew forming on grass at night
steam turning into drops on a cold lid
questions.explanation: Melting, evaporating and boiling happen when heat is added. Freezing and condensing happen when heat is taken away.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: A glass of cold lemon sherbet 'sweats' on a hot day. Put the steps in order.
sequence: Warm air containing invisible water vapour touches the cold glass.
The water vapour cools down.
The water vapour condenses into tiny drops of liquid water.
The drops gather on the outside of the glass.
questions.explanation: Air always holds some invisible water vapour. When the vapour meets a cold surface it cools and condenses. The water comes from the air, not from inside the glass.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Which of these make water evaporate faster? Choose all that are right.
options: a warm, sunny day
a strong breeze
spreading the water out in a wide, thin layer
putting a lid over the water
moving the water into a cold fridge
questions.explanation: Evaporation is faster when it is warmer, windier and when the surface area is larger. A lid traps the vapour and a cold fridge is cooler, so both slow evaporation down.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Which sentence about boiling water is correct?
options: Its temperature keeps rising above 100 °C.
It happens at any temperature.
It happens only at the surface.
Bubbles of water vapour form all through the liquid.
questions.explanation: In boiling, bubbles of water vapour form throughout the liquid, and the temperature stays at 100 °C. Changing only at the surface, at any temperature, describes evaporation.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: When salty water evaporates, the ___ is left behind because it does not ___.
questions.explanation: Only the water turns into a gas. The dissolved salt stays behind as crystals. This is how salt is made from sea water.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Explain the difference between evaporation and boiling.
questions.model_answer: Evaporation happens only at the surface of a liquid and at any temperature. Boiling happens all through the liquid, with bubbles, at the boiling point (100 °C for water).
questions.explanation: Both change a liquid into a gas. Evaporation is slow and only from the surface at any temperature. Boiling is fast, with bubbles forming throughout the liquid, once the boiling point is reached.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Look at the water cycle. Which number shows **evaporation**?
questions.image_alt: The water cycle with five stages numbered: 1 evaporation, 2 condensation, 3 precipitation, 4 collection, 5 transpiration.
questions.explanation: In evaporation (1), the Sun warms liquid water in the sea, rivers and lakes and it turns into water vapour. Condensation (2) is the reverse.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Look at the water cycle. Which number shows water vapour cooling and changing into tiny drops to make clouds?
questions.image_alt: The water cycle with five stages numbered: 1 evaporation, 2 condensation, 3 precipitation, 4 collection, 5 transpiration.
questions.explanation: High in the air it is cold. Water vapour cools and condenses into tiny drops of liquid water, which form clouds. This is condensation (2).

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Chocolate melts at about 30–35 °C. Which thermometer shows a temperature at which chocolate would melt?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C reading 5 °C, 25 °C and 40 °C.
options: A
B
C
questions.explanation: Thermometer C reads 40 °C, which is above the melting point of chocolate. A (5 °C) and B (25 °C) are too cool, so the chocolate stays solid.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Match each picture to the change of state it shows.

pairs.text: ice cream left in the sun

questions.explanation: Ice cream melts when heated. A kettle boils. Water freezes in the freezer. A wet shirt dries by evaporation. Drops on a cold drink are condensation from the air.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Which of these is made when water vapour in the air cools and condenses?
questions.explanation: Fog is made of tiny drops of liquid water that form when water vapour in cool air condenses. Sunshine, wind and fire are not made this way.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Look at the particle pictures and the arrows between them. Heat is taken away from the gas on the right. What happens first?
questions.image_alt: Three boxes of particles: solid on the left (packed in rows), liquid in the middle (touching, jumbled) and gas on the right (far apart). Arrows labelled melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing join them.
options: It condenses into a liquid in the middle.
It melts into a solid on the left.
It evaporates into a liquid in the middle.
It freezes into a solid on the left.
questions.explanation: Removing heat from a gas makes it condense into a liquid, shown by the arrow labelled condensing. The gas must pass through the liquid state before it could freeze.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Mina's mother has washed the school uniforms. Where will they dry fastest?
options: Folded in a pile on a hot, windy day.
Spread out on a line on a hot, windy day.
Spread out on a line on a cool, damp day.
Folded in a bucket in a shady room.
questions.explanation: Warmth, wind and a large surface area all speed up evaporation. Spreading the uniforms out on a hot, windy day gives all three.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Raju takes a cold bottle of water out of the fridge on a hot day. Soon the outside is covered with drops. Where did the drops come from?
options: Water vapour in the air touched the cold bottle and condensed.
Water leaked out through tiny holes in the bottle.
The cold bottle made new water out of the cold.
Water inside the bottle evaporated and stuck to the outside.
questions.explanation: The air around us always holds invisible water vapour. When it touches the cold bottle it cools and condenses into drops. The water does not come from inside the bottle.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Many homes in Bangladesh keep drinking water in a clay pot (kolshi), and the water stays cool. How does the clay pot keep the water cool?
options: Clay makes cold, which flows into the water.
Water seeps to the outside and evaporates, taking heat from the pot.
Water vapour condenses on the inside of the pot.
The pot sends its heat down into the ground.
questions.explanation: A little water seeps through the clay and evaporates from the outer surface. Evaporation takes heat from the pot, so the water inside is cooled.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Moung spreads wet paddy (rice grains) on a mat in the sun. Which actions will help it dry faster? Choose all that are right.
options: spread it in a thin layer
heap it into one big pile
turn it over now and then
cover it with a plastic sheet
put it in the sunniest spot
questions.explanation: A thin layer gives a large surface area, turning brings wet grains to the top, and sunshine adds heat, so the water evaporates faster. A pile or a cover traps the water vapour.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Imran's mother lifts the lid from a pot of boiling rice. The steam is very hot, so she tilts the lid so that the opening faces away from her face and arms. This is the safe thing to do.
questions.explanation: Steam and boiling water can cause bad burns. Lifting the lid away from your body keeps your face and arms out of the hot steam. Young children should ask an adult to do this.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: A climber camps near the top of Mount Everest. Water there boils at only about 70 °C. Why does her rice take so long to cook?
options: Rice cannot soak up water when the air is cold.
There is no water vapour in the air on a mountain.
Boiling water on a mountain is hotter than 100 °C.
The boiling water is cooler than 100 °C, so it cooks the rice more slowly.
questions.explanation: On Everest the air pressure is low, so water boils at about 70 °C instead of 100 °C. Bubbling water that is only 70 °C is not hot enough to cook rice quickly.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: In the simulation, what do the particles do when water is a solid?

sim.task: Open States of Matter Basics and choose the States screen. Choose water, then press the Solid button. Watch the particles for a few seconds.

options: They fly around quickly and far apart.
They slide past each other.
They stay in a fixed pattern and only vibrate.
They stop and do not move at all.
questions.explanation: In a solid the particles are packed in a regular pattern and can only vibrate on the spot. That is why a solid keeps its shape.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: In the simulation, when you add more heat to the water, the particles move faster and the temperature on the thermometer goes up.

sim.task: Open States of Matter Basics and choose the States screen. Choose water and press Liquid. Slowly move the heat/cool control to add heat. Watch how fast the particles move and read the thermometer.

questions.explanation: Heat makes particles move faster, and the thermometer shows a higher temperature. Add enough heat and the liquid changes into a gas.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Start with water as a solid and keep adding heat. Put what you see in order.

sim.task: Open States of Matter Basics and choose the States screen. Choose water and press Solid. Then add heat a little at a time with the heat/cool control, and press Liquid and Gas to compare what the particles do.

sequence: The particles vibrate in fixed places.
The particles break free and slide around each other.
The particles zoom around, far apart.
questions.explanation: Heating makes the particles move faster and faster: solid, then liquid, then gas.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Class 5A heated ice and recorded the temperature every 2 minutes (example results). Time in minutes: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. Temperature in °C: −10, 0, 0, 25, 58, 90, 100, 100. In which 2-minute period did the temperature rise the most?
options: 0 to 2 minutes
6 to 8 minutes
4 to 6 minutes
8 to 10 minutes
questions.explanation: The rises were: 0–2 min +10 °C, 4–6 min +25 °C, 6–8 min +33 °C and 8–10 min +32 °C. The biggest rise was 6 to 8 minutes. The flat parts (2–4 and 12–14 minutes) are melting and boiling.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Tuli watches a boiling kettle. Just above the spout there is a clear gap, and higher up there is a white cloud. What is in the clear gap?
options: invisible water vapour
tiny ice crystals
tiny drops of liquid water
empty space with nothing in it
questions.explanation: Water vapour is a gas and cannot be seen. As it moves away from the spout it cools and condenses into tiny drops of liquid water, and these drops make the white cloud we call steam.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Sea water holds about 3.5 kg of salt in every 100 litres (example numbers). Three salt fields each hold 20 000 litres of sea water. If all the water evaporates, the three fields can make ___ kg of salt.
questions.explanation: One field has 20 000 ÷ 100 = 200 lots of 100 litres, so 200 × 3.5 = 700 kg. Three fields make 3 × 700 = 2100 kg. The salt does not evaporate, so all of it is left behind.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: A beaker of ice and water is heated steadily. The thermometer reads 0 °C for several minutes while the ice melts, even though the burner is still on. Explain why the temperature does not rise.
questions.model_answer: The heat energy is being used to melt the ice (to change it from solid to liquid), not to make the water warmer. When all the ice has melted, the temperature starts to rise again.
questions.explanation: During a change of state, the heat that is added is used to change the state, not to raise the temperature. The same happens at 100 °C while water boils.

questions.title: States of Matter: Evaporation, Condensation, Boiling and Melting
questions.stem: Joy tests whether a wide dish dries faster than a narrow cup. She leaves the dish in the sun for 4 hours with 100 ml of water. She leaves the cup in the shade for 2 hours with 50 ml of water. Which changes would make her test fair? Choose all that are right.
options: Put both containers in the same sunny place.
Start with the same volume of water in each.
Use a dish and a cup of the same width.
Leave both for the same length of time.
Use salty water in one and fresh water in the other.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only one thing changes (the surface area) and everything else stays the same: place, starting volume and time. Using the same width would remove the thing she is testing.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: A **mixture** is…
options: two or more materials mixed together but not joined
a liquid with nothing at all in it
one material that has been heated and cooled
a solid that has changed into a liquid
questions.explanation: In a mixture the materials are only mixed, not joined, so each one keeps its own properties. That is why we can often separate them again.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Match each mixture to the best way to separate it.
questions.explanation: Choose a method that uses a difference between the materials: size (sieve), magnetism (magnet), insoluble solid in a liquid (filter), or a dissolved solid in a liquid (evaporate the water).

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: When sugar dissolves in water, it disappears and is gone for ever.
questions.explanation: The sugar breaks up into pieces too small to see and spreads through the water. It is still there: the water tastes sweet, and you can get the sugar back by evaporating the water.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Sort these materials into those that dissolve in water and those that do not.
questions.explanation: Salt, sugar and instant coffee dissolve to make solutions. Sand, chalk and flour stay as solid pieces in the water, so they can be filtered out.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Sort these changes into reversible and irreversible.
questions.explanation: Melting, freezing and dissolving can be undone because no new material is made. Baking, burning and rusting make new materials, so they cannot be undone.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Rana spilled sand, salt and iron nails into one jar. Put the steps in the best order to get all three back.
sequence: Use a magnet to pull out the iron nails.
Add water and stir so that the salt dissolves.
Filter the mixture: the sand stays in the filter paper.
Evaporate the water from the salty water to get the salt.
questions.explanation: Take out the magnetic nails first. Water dissolves the salt but not the sand, so filtering separates them. Evaporating the water from the filtered solution leaves the salt.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Which of these are signs that a new material has been made? Choose all that are right.
options: bubbles of gas appear
a new colour forms
heat or light is given out
the material is cut into smaller pieces
the material is stirred
questions.explanation: Bubbles of gas, a colour change, a new smell, and heat or light being given out all show that new materials are forming. Cutting and stirring only change the shape or position of a material.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Materials that dissolve in water are called ___, and materials that do not dissolve are called ___.
questions.explanation: Salt and sugar are soluble. Sand and chalk are insoluble. The liquid that forms when a solid dissolves is called a solution.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: When salt dissolves in water we get a salt ___. The salt is still there, so the mass of the solution is the mass of the water ___ the mass of the salt.
questions.explanation: Dissolved salt is not lost. It is spread through the water, so the solution has a mass equal to the water plus the salt.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Salty water goes straight through filter paper, salt and all. Why?
options: The salt has changed into water.
The salt is so heavy that it sinks through the paper.
The dissolved salt is in pieces far too small to be caught by the paper.
The holes in the filter paper are too big for water.
questions.explanation: When salt dissolves it breaks into pieces much smaller than the holes in the filter paper. To get the salt back, evaporate the water instead.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Sumi says: 'When sugar dissolves in water it disappears, so it is gone.' Give two pieces of evidence that the sugar is still there.
questions.model_answer: The water tastes sweet. If you evaporate the water, the sugar is left behind. The solution weighs the same as the water plus the sugar.
questions.explanation: Taste, evaporating the water and measuring the mass all show that the sugar is still present in the solution, even though we cannot see it.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Which of these is an irreversible change?
options: melting chocolate
burning a match
dissolving salt in water
freezing juice
questions.explanation: Burning makes new materials (ash, gases, heat and light) and cannot be undone. Melting, dissolving and freezing can all be reversed.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Look at the picture of filtering muddy water. Which number shows the sand left behind (the residue)?
questions.image_alt: Filtering muddy water with a funnel and filter paper, with five parts numbered.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is the sand left behind in the filter paper. The clear water that passes through is number 4.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Use the picture of the filtering equipment. Put the steps for filtering sandy water in order.
questions.image_alt: A funnel with filter paper over a beaker, with sand left in the paper and clear water in the beaker.
sequence: Fold the filter paper and put it in the funnel.
Stand the funnel over a beaker.
Pour the sandy water slowly into the funnel.
Clear water drips into the beaker and the sand stays in the paper.
questions.explanation: The filter paper must be in place before you pour. The liquid passes through the tiny holes in the paper, but the insoluble sand is too big and stays behind.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into reversible and irreversible changes.
questions.explanation: Melting and dissolving can be undone by cooling or evaporating. Cooking an egg, bread or rice makes new materials, and you can never turn them back into the raw food.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Which tool is best for pulling iron nails out of a pile of sand?
questions.explanation: Iron is magnetic and sand is not, so a magnet pulls out only the nails. Scissors, a spoon or a magnifying glass cannot tell the two materials apart.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Rana pours sandy salt water into the funnel in the picture. What collects in the beaker (5)?
questions.image_alt: Filtering with a funnel, filter paper, sand left behind and a beaker of clear liquid below.
options: pure water with no salt
sandy water
salty water with no sand
dry salt crystals
questions.explanation: The sand is insoluble and stays in the filter paper. The salt is dissolved in tiny pieces and goes through with the water, so the beaker holds salty water.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Which of these will dissolve in water?
questions.explanation: Salt is soluble, so it dissolves in water to make a solution. Rock, brick and wood are insoluble.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Farmers toss rice in a flat bamboo tray called a kula, in the breeze. The grains fall back into the tray but the husks blow away. Why?
options: The tray has holes that only the husks can fit through.
The husks dissolve in the moving air.
The grains are magnetic and are pulled back to the tray.
The wind blows the light husks away, but the heavy grains fall back.
questions.explanation: Rice grains and husks have different masses. The wind can carry the light husks, but the heavier grains fall straight back down.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Nadia stirs a spoon of sugar into her hot cha and the sugar seems to disappear. Where is the sugar now?
options: It has changed into water.
It has dissolved and is spread through the cha.
It has floated to the top of the cha.
It has been destroyed.
questions.explanation: Dissolved sugar is broken into tiny pieces that spread through the liquid. The cha tastes sweet because the sugar is still there.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Moung filters muddy pond water through a clean cloth and the water looks clear. It is now safe to drink.
questions.explanation: Filtering removes mud and other solid pieces. Germs and dissolved substances are far too small to be caught by the cloth, so the water still needs to be boiled or properly treated.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: On a winter morning in Jashore, a neighbour offers Arif a cup of fresh, raw date palm sap that was filtered through cloth. What should Arif do?
options: Drink it, because the cloth has removed everything harmful.
Leave it in a warm place for a few hours and drink it later.
Drink just a small sip, to test it.
Say no politely, and say that sap should be boiled before anyone drinks it.
questions.explanation: Cloth can remove insects and bark, but a virus is far too small to be stopped by it. Health experts in Bangladesh say never to drink raw date palm sap, because bats can contaminate it. Boiling makes it safe.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Rafi bakes a cake. After it has cooled, he can change it back into flour, eggs and sugar.
questions.explanation: Baking makes new materials. The cake rises because gas bubbles form, the colour and smell change, and the ingredients cannot be taken back out. It is an irreversible change.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Priya wants one spoon of sugar to dissolve quickly in a glass of water. Which actions will help? Choose all that are right.
options: stir the water
use fine sugar instead of big lumps
use warmer water
leave it without stirring
use bigger sugar crystals
questions.explanation: Stirring, smaller pieces and warmer water all make dissolving faster. Leaving it still or using big crystals slows it down.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Class 5B timed how long one teaspoon of sugar took to dissolve in 100 ml of water at different temperatures (example results). At 10 °C it took 180 s, at 25 °C 95 s, at 40 °C 50 s and at 60 °C 25 s. What is the best prediction for the time at 50 °C?
options: about 15 seconds
about 35 seconds
about 75 seconds
about 100 seconds
questions.explanation: The time falls as the water gets warmer. 50 °C lies between 40 °C (50 s) and 60 °C (25 s), so the time must lie between 25 s and 50 s: about 35 seconds.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Using the same results (10 °C: 180 s, 25 °C: 95 s, 40 °C: 50 s, 60 °C: 25 s), the sugar took ___ seconds longer to dissolve at 10 °C than at 60 °C.
questions.explanation: 180 − 25 = 155 seconds. Cold water dissolves sugar much more slowly than hot water.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Class 5B timed each temperature only once. How could they make their results more reliable?
questions.model_answer: Repeat the test at each temperature several times (for example three times) and work out the average (mean) time.
questions.explanation: One result might be wrong because of a mistake or a slow stopwatch. Repeating the test and finding the average makes the results more reliable.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Joy puts 200 g of water in a cup and stirs in 15 g of salt until it has all dissolved (example numbers). The salty water has a mass of ___ g.
questions.explanation: The salt is still there, just spread through the water, so the masses add: 200 + 15 = 215 g.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Rafi mixes iron filings, chalk powder and sugar. He stirs the mixture into water and filters it. What is left on the filter paper?
options: iron filings and sugar
sugar and chalk powder
iron filings and chalk powder
only chalk powder
questions.explanation: Sugar is soluble, so it dissolves and goes through the paper with the water. Iron filings and chalk are insoluble and stay behind. Rafi could then use a magnet to pull out the iron.

questions.title: Mixtures, Solutions and Changes
questions.stem: Imran says: 'A burning candle is just wax melting, so the change is reversible.' Which observation shows that this is not the whole story?
options: The flame gives out heat and light and the candle slowly gets smaller.
The wax near the flame is soft and runny.
The melted wax goes hard again when it cools.
The candle is made from a solid material.
questions.explanation: Melted wax that sets again is reversible. But burning also uses up wax to make new substances and gives out heat and light, and that part cannot be undone.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: All matter is made of tiny building blocks called…
options: cells
atoms
droplets
crystals
questions.explanation: Air, water, your desk and your body are all made of atoms. Atoms are so small that a single human hair is about half a million atoms wide.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: A material made of only one kind of atom is an ___. When atoms join together they make a ___.
questions.explanation: Oxygen, iron and gold are elements. A water molecule is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Match each key word to its meaning.
pairs: the tiny building block of matter
made of only one kind of atom
nothing can get in or out
questions.explanation: These key words describe matter and how we study it. The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons, with the electrons moving around it.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: When sugar dissolves in water, its atoms are destroyed.
questions.explanation: No atoms are destroyed in any physical or chemical change. The sugar atoms are still there, spread through the water.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: 330 g of juice is frozen to make an ice lolly. The ice lolly has a mass of ___ g.
questions.explanation: Freezing only rearranges how the particles are arranged. No atoms are gained or lost, so the mass stays at 330 g.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Sort these into elements and substances made of different atoms joined together.
questions.explanation: Iron, gold and aluminium are each made of only one kind of atom. Water has hydrogen and oxygen atoms joined, and carbon dioxide has carbon and oxygen atoms joined.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Which of these is a closed system?
options: an open pan of boiling water
a candle burning in a room
a puddle drying in the sun
a sealed jar
questions.explanation: In a closed system nothing can get in or out. A sealed jar keeps everything inside, while open pans, candles and puddles can lose gases to the air.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Vinegar and baking soda react in a sealed bag and the bag puffs up with gas. Which of these stay the same? Choose all that are right.
options: the total number of atoms
the total mass of the bag and its contents
the kinds of atom present
the substances inside the bag
the way the atoms are joined together
questions.explanation: In a chemical change atoms are rearranged but none are made or destroyed, so the atom count, the kinds of atom and the total mass stay the same. The substances and how atoms are joined do change.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: What happens to the total amount of energy in a closed system?
options: The total stays the same; energy only moves or changes form.
Energy is made new whenever something moves.
The energy slowly disappears into the air.
Some energy is destroyed every time it changes form.
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be made or destroyed. It moves from place to place or changes form, for example from electrical energy to light and heat.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: A candle has a mass of 50 g. After burning for an hour its mass is 42 g. Has mass been destroyed? Explain.
questions.model_answer: No. The wax reacted with oxygen and turned into carbon dioxide gas and water vapour, which escaped into the air because the candle was in an open system.
questions.explanation: The atoms of wax were rearranged into gases that drifted into the air, so the candle lost mass. If you caught all the gases in a sealed container, the total mass would not change.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Class 5C want to check whether mass is conserved in a reaction. Which tool do they need?
questions.explanation: A balance measures mass. The class weigh everything before the reaction and again after, then compare the two readings.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Which of these gets its heat from splitting big uranium atoms?
questions.explanation: In a nuclear power plant, uranium atoms are split into smaller atoms of other elements, which gives out a huge amount of heat. A campfire and a candle burn fuel, which is a chemical change.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Match each picture to what happens to its atoms.
pairs: small hydrogen atoms join to make helium
big uranium atoms split into smaller atoms
atoms rearrange into gases, smoke and ash
the same molecules, just moving around more
questions.explanation: Nuclear changes in the Sun and in a power plant change the nucleus, so one element turns into another. Burning rearranges atoms, and melting only changes how the molecules move.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into physical, chemical and nuclear changes.

items.text: uranium atoms splitting in a power plant
hydrogen atoms joining in the Sun

questions.explanation: In a physical change atoms just move around. In a chemical change atoms are rearranged to make new substances. In a nuclear change the nucleus itself changes.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Put the steps of making electricity in a nuclear power station in order.

sequence.text: Uranium atoms split in the reactor.
A lot of heat is released.
The heat boils water into steam.
The turbine turns a generator, making electricity.

questions.explanation: Splitting uranium atoms releases heat. The heat makes steam, the steam spins the turbine, and the turbine drives the generator. Energy changes form at each step, but none is lost.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: The picture shows water as a solid, a liquid and a gas. Changing from one box to the next only changes how the particles are arranged and move. No atoms are lost or made.
questions.image_alt: Three boxes of water particles: solid on the left (packed in rows), liquid in the middle (touching), gas on the right (far apart), joined by arrows labelled melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing.
questions.explanation: Melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing are physical changes. The same atoms are present in every box, just arranged and moving differently.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Nadia boils water in an open pot. After 20 minutes the pot and water weigh less. Where did the missing mass go?
options: It sank into the bottom of the pot.
The water was destroyed.
It turned into rice.
It escaped into the air as water vapour.
questions.explanation: Boiling turns liquid water into water vapour, which drifts away from the open pot. No atoms are destroyed; they are just in the air now.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Rafi weighs a shiny iron nail. After some weeks in a damp place it is covered in rust and weighs a little more. Where does the extra mass come from?
options: The nail makes new iron atoms.
The rust is lighter, so the nail should weigh less.
Iron atoms join with oxygen (and water) from the air.
A bit of dust settles on the nail.
questions.explanation: Rust is a new substance made when iron atoms join with oxygen from the air. The added atoms add mass. Nothing is created from nothing.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Tuli makes sherbet by stirring 20 g of sugar into 250 g of water. She says the sherbet should have a mass of 270 g.
questions.explanation: The sugar dissolves but its atoms are still there. The mass of the solution is the water plus the sugar: 250 g + 20 g = 270 g.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Class 5C react vinegar and baking soda in a zip-lock bag on a balance. What is the safest way to do the experiment?
options: Smell the gas closely to check what it is.
Wear goggles and point the bag away from faces.
Taste the mixture to see what it is like.
Squeeze the bag hard so that it fizzes more.
questions.explanation: Vinegar can sting eyes, and a puffed-up bag could burst. Goggles and pointing the bag away keep everyone safe. We never taste or sniff closely in science.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Bangladesh is building its first nuclear power plant at Rooppur, beside the Padma. Which of these are advantages of nuclear power? Choose all that are right.
options: a lot of energy from a little fuel
almost no carbon dioxide while the plant works
steady power day and night
used fuel stays radioactive for thousands of years
it is very expensive to build
questions.explanation: Nuclear plants give a lot of energy from a small amount of uranium and almost no carbon dioxide, and they run day and night. The last two choices are disadvantages.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: In the simulation, you give the sandwich maker far more cheese than the recipe can use. What do you see in the After box?

sim.task: Open Reactants, Products and Leftovers and choose the Sandwiches screen. Pick a recipe. In the Before box, use the sliders to give a large number of cheese slices and only a few of the other ingredients. Look at the After box.

options: The extra cheese disappears.
The sandwich maker makes more sandwiches than the recipe allows.
The extra cheese turns into bread.
Some cheese is left over after the sandwiches are made.
questions.explanation: Each sandwich needs a fixed amount of each ingredient. Ingredients that are not used up are the leftovers. Nothing disappears.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: In the simulation, the slices of bread you start with always equal the slices of bread in the sandwiches plus the bread slices left over.

sim.task: Open Reactants, Products and Leftovers and choose the Sandwiches screen. Pick a recipe and set the number of bread, cheese and meat slices in the Before box. Count the bread slices before. Then count the bread in the sandwiches plus any bread left over after. Try two different settings.

questions.explanation: The sandwich model shows conservation: ingredients (like atoms) are only rearranged into sandwiches, and the ones not used are leftovers. None are made or lost.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: In the sandwich model, match each science word to what it means.

sim.task: Open Reactants, Products and Leftovers and choose the Sandwiches screen. Look at the Before box and the After box and think about what each one shows.

pairs: ingredients that are not used up
questions.explanation: In a chemical reaction the reactants are rearranged to make products. Any reactant that is not used up is a leftover.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Example: a nucleus with 235 protons and neutrons is hit by 1 free neutron, then splits into pieces with 139 and 94 protons and neutrons, plus 3 free neutrons. Before: 235 + 1 = ___. After: 139 + 94 + 3 = ___.
questions.explanation: Both totals are 236, so the total number of protons plus neutrons is conserved, even though one element has changed into others.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Example: a nucleus with 236 protons and neutrons splits into two pieces with 140 and 94 protons and neutrons, and some free neutrons. If the total number of protons and neutrons is conserved, how many free neutrons are released?
questions.explanation: The two pieces have 140 + 94 = 234. To reach the original 236, there must be 236 − 234 = 2 free neutrons.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Which statement about chemical changes and nuclear changes is correct?
options: Atoms are not conserved in either kind of change.
Atoms are conserved in both chemical changes and nuclear changes.
In chemical changes atoms are only rearranged, but in nuclear changes one kind of atom changes into another.
Nothing at all is conserved in a nuclear change.
questions.explanation: Chemical changes rearrange the same atoms. Nuclear changes alter the nucleus, so one element becomes another. Even so, the total number of protons plus neutrons stays the same.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Class 5C measured mass before and after (example results). Salt dissolving in an open cup: 270 g then 270 g. Vinegar and baking soda in a sealed bag: 312 g then 312 g. The same reaction in an open cup: 312 g then 309 g. What best explains the 3 g lost from the open cup?
options: A gas made in the reaction escaped into the air.
Atoms were destroyed, but only in an open cup.
The balance gives lower readings when a cup is open.
The salt dissolving took away some mass.
questions.explanation: The reaction made a gas (carbon dioxide). In the sealed bag the gas could not escape, so the mass stayed 312 g. In the open cup the gas escaped, taking 3 g of mass with it.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Explain why scientists say atoms are conserved in chemical changes but not in nuclear changes, and say what is still conserved in a nuclear change.
questions.model_answer: In chemical changes atoms are only rearranged, so the same atoms are there before and after. In nuclear changes the nucleus changes, so atoms of one element turn into another. The total number of protons plus neutrons is still the same.
questions.explanation: Chemical changes only move atoms into new groups. Nuclear changes alter the atoms themselves, but counting all the protons and neutrons gives the same total before and after.

questions.title: Matter, Atoms and Conservation
questions.stem: Example: of every 10 units of electrical energy a light bulb uses, 2 units become light. In a closed system the other ___ units must become heat.
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved: the total must stay at 10 units. 10 − 2 = 8 units, so 8 units become heat.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Which form of energy is stored in food?
options: chemical
electrical
light
sound
questions.explanation: Food, fuel and batteries store chemical energy. Our bodies change the chemical energy in food into movement and heat.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Sort these by the main form of energy they have or give out.
questions.explanation: Moving things have kinetic energy. Food and batteries store chemical energy. A firefly gives out light and a drum gives out sound.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Match each device to the energy change it makes.
questions.explanation: Every device transforms energy from one form into another. Some of the energy always ends up as heat that we do not need.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Energy cannot be created or ___. It can only move from place to place or change ___.
questions.explanation: This is the law of conservation of energy. The total amount of energy stays the same; it is only moved or transformed.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Heat moves from a hotter object to a colder object.
questions.explanation: Heat is energy that always flows from hotter things to colder things. That is why a hot cup of tea cools down until it reaches room temperature.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: A ball bounces lower and lower and then stops. Where has its energy gone?
options: It was destroyed when the ball stopped moving.
It spread out as heat and sound.
It is still inside the ball as movement energy.
It was changed into light energy that we cannot see.
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be destroyed. Each time the ball hits the ground, some of its energy spreads out as heat and sound, so the ball has less energy for bouncing.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Which of these materials are good thermal insulators? Choose all that are right.
options: wood
wool
plastic
iron
copper
questions.explanation: Insulators such as wood, wool, plastic and trapped air slow heat down. Metals like iron and copper are thermal conductors that let heat pass easily.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: A solar panel changes ___ energy into ___ energy.
questions.explanation: Sunlight shining on a solar panel is changed into electrical energy. A little heat is given out too.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: An LED bulb is more efficient than an old filament bulb because it wastes less energy as heat.
questions.explanation: An LED bulb gives the same light as a filament bulb but uses only about one fifth of the electricity. More of its energy becomes light and less is wasted as heat.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Explain why a metal spoon in hot tea gets hot quickly, but a wooden spoon does not.
questions.model_answer: Metal is a thermal conductor, so heat moves through it easily. Wood is a thermal insulator, so heat moves through it slowly.
questions.explanation: Metals are thermal conductors and carry heat along them quickly. Wood slows heat down, so the end you hold stays cool for much longer.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: When a ceiling fan is switched off, its energy has been destroyed.
questions.explanation: Energy is never destroyed. When the fan stops, its movement energy has spread out into the surroundings, mostly as heat and sound.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: The four cups hold the same hot water. One is uncovered and the others are wrapped in newspaper, wool or foil. Which cup would you expect to stay hot the longest?
questions.image_alt: Four cups of hot water: one with no cover and the others wrapped in newspaper, wool and foil.
options: the uncovered cup
the cup wrapped in newspaper
the cup wrapped in foil
the cup wrapped in wool
questions.explanation: Wool traps lots of air, and air is a poor conductor of heat, so heat escapes slowly. It is the best insulator of these materials.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: In this fair test of four cups, which cup is the control that the others are compared with?
questions.image_alt: Four cups of hot water: one with no cover and the others wrapped in newspaper, wool and foil.
options: the cup in wool
the cup in newspaper
the uncovered cup
the cup in foil
questions.explanation: The uncovered cup shows how fast hot water cools with no insulation at all. It is the comparison for the three wrapped cups.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Match each picture to the main energy it gives out.
questions.explanation: A loudspeaker gives out sound, a bulb gives out light, a fan makes air move and a hot drink gives out heat.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into things that are moving and things that store energy.
questions.explanation: Moving things have kinetic energy. Batteries, food and fuels such as wood store chemical energy until it is released.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Which picture shows a device that changes sunlight into electricity?
questions.explanation: A solar panel changes light energy from the Sun into electrical energy. A wind turbine uses moving air, and candles and kettles use chemical or electrical energy.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: The three thermometers show the temperatures of three cups of water. Cup A and cup C are placed touching in a closed box. Which way does heat move?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C reading 12 °C, 37 °C and 48 °C.
options: from cup A to cup C
from cup C to cup A
nowhere, because both are water
in both directions equally
questions.explanation: Cup C (48 °C) is hotter than cup A (12 °C), so heat moves from C to A. Cup C loses heat and cools, and cup A gains heat and warms, until they are the same temperature.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Rafi eats a plate of rice and then pedals his rickshaw all day. Which energy chain describes this?
options: kinetic (food) → chemical (rickshaw) + heat
light (food) → electrical (rickshaw) + sound
chemical (food) → kinetic (rickshaw) + heat
electrical (food) → sound (rickshaw) + light
questions.explanation: The chemical energy stored in food is changed into movement energy, and some becomes heat. This is why we feel warm when we work hard.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Cooking pots in many kitchens are made of metal, but their handles are made of wood or plastic. Why?
options: Wood and plastic are insulators, so the handle stays cool.
Wood and plastic are conductors, so heat reaches the food faster.
Metal handles would be too heavy, so the pot would tip over.
Wood and plastic make the food inside heat up more quickly.
questions.explanation: Metal is a good thermal conductor, so heat passes quickly from the flame to the food. Wood and plastic are insulators and slow heat down, which keeps the handle safe to hold.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: A village home in Bangladesh has a solar home system. Put the energy steps in order, from day to night.
sequence: Sunlight shines on the solar panel on the roof.
The panel changes the light energy into electrical energy.
The battery stores the energy as chemical energy.
At night the battery supplies electrical energy.
The LED light changes the electrical energy into light (and a little heat).
questions.explanation: The panel works in the daytime and the battery stores the energy for the night. At every step energy is changed in form and a little is wasted as heat, but none is destroyed.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Mina wants her soup to stay hot until lunch. Which of these will help? Choose all that are right.
options: put it in an insulated flask
wrap the container in a woollen cloth
keep the lid on
leave the lid off in a cool breeze
pour it into a thin metal cup
questions.explanation: Insulators such as a flask, wool and a lid slow the loss of heat. An open lid in a breeze and a thin metal cup let heat escape quickly.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: A metal spoon has been left in a pot on the stove. Tuli says it is safe to grab it with bare hands because metal stays cool.
questions.explanation: Metal is a thermal conductor, so heat travels quickly along the spoon and it becomes very hot. Use a dry cloth or pot holder, which are insulators, and take care.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Put the energy changes in order for the cyclist lighting a bulb.

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Systems screen. Choose the cyclist as the energy source, the generator as the energy changer and the light bulb as the energy user. Switch the cyclist on and watch the energy symbols move.

sequence: The cyclist changes chemical energy from food into movement of the pedals.
The pedals turn the generator.
The generator changes movement energy into electrical energy.
The bulb changes the electrical energy into light and heat.
questions.explanation: Energy moves along the chain and changes form at each step. The bulb gives out light and some heat, and the total energy stays the same.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: What happens to the temperature of the water in the beaker?

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Intro screen. Drag the beaker of water above one of the burners. Slide the burner control up to Heat for a while and watch the thermometer. Then slide it down to Cool for a while and watch again.

options: It falls when heated and rises when it is cooled.
It rises when heated and falls when cooled.
It stays the same either way.
It rises both when heated and when cooled.
questions.explanation: When the water gains heat its temperature rises, and when it loses heat its temperature falls.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: What happens to the atoms and the temperature as you rub the books together?

sim.task: Open Friction. Drag the top book so that it rubs back and forth across the bottom book for a while. Watch the atoms and the thermometer.

options: The atoms jiggle faster and the temperature rises.
The atoms stop moving and the temperature stays the same.
The atoms jiggle slower and the temperature falls.
The atoms disappear and the temperature falls.
questions.explanation: Your movement energy is transferred to the atoms, which jiggle faster. Faster-moving atoms mean the books are warmer: movement energy has changed into thermal energy.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Class 5D poured 200 ml of water at 80 °C into identical cups (example results). After 20 minutes the temperatures were: no cover 52 °C, newspaper 60 °C, wool 68 °C, foil 58 °C. The uncovered cup cooled by ___ °C more than the cup wrapped in wool.
questions.explanation: The uncovered cup cooled by 80 − 52 = 28 °C, and the wool cup by 80 − 68 = 12 °C. The difference is 28 − 12 = 16 °C. Wool is the best insulator.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: A filament bulb uses 25 W. An LED bulb that gives the same light uses about one fifth as much (example numbers). Energy used (Wh) = power (W) × time (h). How much less electrical energy does the LED use in 4 hours?
options: 20 Wh
80 Wh
100 Wh
5 Wh
questions.explanation: The LED uses 25 ÷ 5 = 5 W. In 4 hours the filament bulb uses 25 × 4 = 100 Wh and the LED uses 5 × 4 = 20 Wh. The saving is 100 − 20 = 80 Wh, because the LED wastes much less energy as heat.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: Energy (Wh) = power (W) × time (h). A 50 W solar panel gets 5 hours of good sunshine, so it makes 250 Wh a day (example numbers). A family uses three 5 W LED bulbs for 4 hours and a 20 W fan for 6 hours. How much energy is left to charge phones?
options: 130 Wh
70 Wh
180 Wh
250 Wh
questions.explanation: Bulbs: 3 × 5 × 4 = 60 Wh. Fan: 20 × 6 = 120 Wh. Total used 180 Wh. Energy left: 250 − 180 = 70 Wh, enough to charge a phone.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
