questions.stem: 'We should save energy, but energy cannot be destroyed.' Explain why both statements can be true.
questions.model_answer: Energy is never destroyed, but useful energy such as fuel or electricity gets changed into heat that spreads out and cannot be used again. Saving energy means using less of the limited useful energy, which costs money and may run out.
questions.explanation: The total amount of energy stays the same, but much of it ends up as spread-out heat that is no longer useful to us. Fuels are limited, so using less of them saves useful energy.

questions.title: Energy and Its Transformations
questions.stem: An uncovered cup of water cooled from 80 °C to 52 °C in 20 minutes (example data). The room stays at 30 °C all night. What will the temperature of the water be next morning?
options: about 52 °C
about 0 °C
about 80 °C
about 30 °C
questions.explanation: The water loses heat to the room until it reaches the same temperature as the room, 30 °C. It cannot become colder than the room without a fridge or ice.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Every sound starts with a ___. It travels as a ___ and cannot travel through empty ___.
questions.explanation: A vibrating object pushes on the particles next to it, and the vibration passes along as a sound wave. In empty space there are no particles, so sound cannot travel.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Match each sound source to the part that vibrates.
pairs: the vocal cords in your throat
questions.explanation: Hitting, plucking and blowing make different parts vibrate. When you hum, you can feel the vibration of your vocal cords with your fingers on your throat.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Sound travels faster through steel than through air.
questions.explanation: Sound travels at about 340 metres per second in air, 1500 in water and 5900 in steel. Particles in solids are closer together, so they pass the vibrations on faster.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Astronauts standing on the Moon can hear each other talk without radios.
questions.explanation: The Moon has no air, so there are no particles to pass the vibrations along. Sound cannot travel through empty space, so astronauts use radios.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Sort these changes by what they do to the pitch of a string instrument.
questions.explanation: Short, tight, thin strings vibrate faster (a higher frequency), so they make a higher pitch. Long, loose, thick strings vibrate more slowly and make a lower pitch.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how you hear a sound.
sequence: The outer ear collects the sound.
The sound goes down the ear canal.
The eardrum vibrates.
Three tiny bones pass the vibrations on.
The cochlea turns them into messages.
A nerve carries the messages to the brain.
questions.explanation: The eardrum is a thin skin that vibrates when sound reaches it. The tiny bones pass the vibrations to the cochlea, which sends messages along a nerve to the brain.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: The number of vibrations each second is called the frequency. It is measured in…
options: decibels (dB)
metres per second
newtons
hertz (Hz)
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). A frequency of 100 Hz means 100 vibrations every second. Decibels measure loudness, not pitch.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Which of these would change the **pitch** of a guitar string? Choose all that are right.
options: making the string shorter
making the string tighter
using a thinner string
plucking the string harder
plucking the string gently
questions.explanation: Length, tightness and thickness change how fast the string vibrates, and so the pitch. Plucking harder or more gently only changes the size of the vibrations, which changes loudness.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: On a wave diagram, what shows how loud the sound is?
options: how long the diagram is
how close together the waves are
the height of the wave
the colour of the line
questions.explanation: Taller waves mean bigger vibrations and a louder sound. How close the waves are together shows the pitch.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Why do we see lightning before we hear the thunder?
questions.model_answer: Light travels much faster than sound, so the light reaches us first and the sound arrives later.
questions.explanation: Light travels almost instantly, but sound travels at only about 340 metres per second in air. The further away the storm, the longer the gap.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Which number is the eardrum, the thin skin that vibrates when sound reaches it?
questions.image_alt: A cross-section of the ear with parts numbered 1 to 6.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is the eardrum. It sits at the end of the ear canal (2) and vibrates when sound waves hit it.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Which number is the part that turns vibrations into messages for the brain?
questions.image_alt: A cross-section of the ear with parts numbered 1 to 6.
questions.explanation: The cochlea (5) turns vibrations into messages. A nerve (6) then carries the messages to the brain. The tiny bones (4) only pass the vibrations on.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Which wave shows the **quietest** sound with the **highest** pitch?
questions.image_alt: Four sound wave drawings A to D that differ in height and in how close the waves are.
options: A
B
C
D
questions.explanation: Short waves mean a quiet sound and waves close together mean a high pitch. Wave D has short waves that are close together.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Look at the four wave pictures. Match each wave to the sound it shows.
questions.image_alt: Four sound wave drawings A to D that differ in height and in how close the waves are.
questions.explanation: Height shows loudness: A and C are tall (loud), B and D are short (quiet). Closeness shows pitch: C and D have waves close together (high), A and B have waves far apart (low).

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Use the decibel scale. Which sounds could damage hearing if you heard them for a long time? Choose all that are right.
questions.image_alt: A decibel scale from 0 to 140 with leaves 20 dB, birds 40, talking 60, traffic 80, loud music 100 and a plane 120. Sounds above 85 dB are shaded.
options: leaves rustling
talking
traffic
loud music
a plane taking off
questions.explanation: Sounds above about 85 dB can permanently damage hearing. Loud music (100 dB) and a plane (120 dB) are in the shaded danger zone. Traffic, at 80 dB, is just below it.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Look at the three instruments. Which one makes its sound when the air inside it vibrates?
questions.image_alt: A dhol (drum), an ektara (string instrument) and a bansuri (flute).
options: the dhol (drum)
the bansuri (flute)
the ektara (string)
questions.explanation: In a bansuri, blowing across the hole makes the column of air inside vibrate. In the dhol it is the drum skin, and in the ektara it is the string.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: An ektara player squeezes the bamboo neck to make the string tighter. What happens to the pitch?
options: It gets higher, because the string vibrates faster.
It gets lower, because the string vibrates slower.
It gets louder, because the vibrations are bigger.
It stays the same, because the string has not got any shorter.
questions.explanation: A tighter string vibrates faster, so its frequency and pitch go up. Loudness depends on how hard the string is plucked.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Whales can hear each other across hundreds of kilometres of ocean. Which fact helps to explain this?
options: Sound travels well and fast through water.
Whale calls travel through the air above the waves.
Light travels through the ocean at the same speed as sound.
Sound is slower in water than in air, so it lasts longer.
questions.explanation: The particles of water are close together, so they pass vibrations along quickly and sound carries a long way. Sound travels about 1500 metres per second in water compared with 340 in air.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Rafi's friend listens to loud music through headphones for hours every day. What is the best advice?
options: Turn the volume up so that the quiet parts can be heard.
Keep the volume as it is, because ears get used to it.
Only music with a low pitch can harm hearing.
Turn the volume down and take breaks.
questions.explanation: Sounds louder than about 85 dB, heard for a long time, can permanently damage hearing. Ears do not get used to loud sound, and it is loudness, not pitch, that causes the harm.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Bangladesh's noise rules make the areas around hospitals and schools silent zones with low noise limits, because loud noise can harm health and learning.
questions.explanation: Noise can cause hearing loss, headaches, stress and poor sleep, and it makes it harder for children to concentrate. Silent zones near hospitals and schools protect people, with limits as low as 50 dB in the daytime.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: A busy road runs past a school in Dhaka. Which actions would help to make a quiet school zone? Choose all that are right.
options: put up 'No horn' signs near the school
plant trees and build a wall beside the road
hang curtains in the classrooms
let drivers use loud hydraulic horns
move band practice next to the road
questions.explanation: Signs reduce horn use, and trees and walls block or absorb sound. Soft curtains absorb sound inside the classroom. Loud horns and extra noise make the problem worse.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: In the simulation, when you increase the frequency, the waves are drawn closer together and the sound has a higher pitch.

sim.task: Open Sound Waves and choose the Single Source screen. Turn the sound on so that you can hear the speaker. Move the frequency slider from low to high and listen. Watch how close together the waves are.

questions.explanation: A higher frequency means more vibrations each second. The waves are closer together and the pitch is higher.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: What happens to the sound when you increase the amplitude and keep the frequency the same?

sim.task: Open Sound Waves and choose the Single Source screen. Turn the sound on. Keep the frequency slider where it is. Move the amplitude slider from low to high, and listen and watch the waves.

options: It gets louder and the pitch goes up.
It gets quieter; the pitch stays the same.
It gets louder; the pitch stays the same.
It gets louder and the pitch goes down.
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the size of the vibrations. Bigger vibrations make a louder sound with taller waves. Pitch depends only on frequency, so it does not change.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: What happens to the sound as the air is taken out of the box around the speaker?

sim.task: Open Sound Waves and choose the Air Pressure screen. Turn the sound on and listen. Then use the pump to take the air out of the box around the speaker, and listen again.

options: It gets louder, because the speaker has more space to move in.
It gets quieter, because fewer particles pass on the vibrations.
It stays the same, because the speaker keeps vibrating just as much.
It gets higher in pitch, because there is less air.
questions.explanation: Sound needs particles to pass the vibrations along. With less air there are fewer particles, so less sound reaches your ear. In a vacuum there would be no sound at all.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: In the simulation, on both the Water screen and the Sound screen, a bigger amplitude makes taller waves.

sim.task: Open Waves Intro. On the Water screen, move the amplitude slider up and watch the waves. Then choose the Sound screen, turn the sound on, and move the amplitude slider up again.

questions.explanation: Amplitude is the size of the wave. A bigger amplitude gives taller water waves and a louder sound. Waves on different screens follow the same rule.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: You hear thunder 3 seconds after you see the lightning. Sound travels about 340 metres each second in air, so the storm is about ___ metres away.
questions.explanation: Light reaches you almost at once, so the 3 seconds is the time taken by the sound. Distance = 340 m/s × 3 s = 1020 m, which is just over 1 km.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Tania twanged a ruler over the edge of a table and a sound app measured the frequency (example results). With 10 cm over the edge it was 120 Hz, 15 cm gave 55 Hz, 20 cm gave 30 Hz and 25 cm gave 20 Hz. What is the best prediction for 12 cm?
options: about 90 Hz
about 40 Hz
about 20 Hz
about 130 Hz
questions.explanation: The frequency falls as more ruler sticks out. 12 cm lies between 10 cm (120 Hz) and 15 cm (55 Hz), so the frequency must lie between 55 and 120 Hz. About 90 Hz fits.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: A class measured the loudness at four places with a sound meter app (example readings): school library 35 dB, classroom 60 dB, busy road outside school 85 dB, bus horn nearby 110 dB. A silent zone near a school can have a limit as low as 50 dB in the daytime. Which places are louder than this limit? Choose all that are right.
options: school library
classroom
busy road outside school
bus horn nearby
questions.explanation: Only the library (35 dB) is below 50 dB. The classroom (60), busy road (85) and bus horn (110) are all above it. The road and the horn are also loud enough to harm hearing over time.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: Explain why a very loud horn can harm the ear. Use what you know about the eardrum.
questions.model_answer: A very loud sound makes very big vibrations. These make the eardrum and the tiny parts of the cochlea vibrate very strongly, which can damage them and cause hearing loss.
questions.explanation: Loudness depends on the size of the vibrations. Very large vibrations can damage the eardrum and the delicate cochlea, and the damage can be permanent.

questions.title: Sound
questions.stem: A boy taps a long steel rail. His sister at the far end hears two taps: one through the rail and one through the air. Which tap does she hear first, and why?
options: They arrive together, because they come from the same tap.
The tap through the air, because air is lighter and easier to move.
The tap through the rail, because steel carries vibrations faster.
The tap through the air, because it is louder.
questions.explanation: Sound travels at about 5900 metres per second in steel but only 340 in air. The vibrations in the steel get to her ear first, and the sound through the air arrives later.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Simple machines help us by changing…
options: the mass of the load that is lifted
the amount of material in the machine
the size or the direction of a force
the gravity pulling on the load
questions.explanation: A machine can make a force smaller, bigger or point a different way. It does not change the load’s mass or the pull of gravity.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Match each simple machine to an example.
questions.explanation: A see-saw is a lever, a flagpole uses a pulley, a rickshaw wheel is a wheel and axle, a ramp is an inclined plane, an axe is a wedge and a jar lid has a screw thread.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Sort the examples by the simple machine they use.
questions.explanation: Levers turn on a pivot. Wedges are two ramps back to back that cut or split. A wheel and axle is a big wheel fixed to a thin rod, as in a knob or a screwdriver handle.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: A lever turns on a ___. A ___ is a wheel with a rope that can change the direction of a force.
questions.explanation: The pivot (fulcrum) is the point a lever turns on. A pulley lets you pull down to lift a load up.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: A ramp lets you lift a heavy load with less force, but you must push it a longer way.
questions.explanation: A ramp trades distance for force. The path is longer, so each push can be smaller.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: The dheki is a long beam on a pivot. A person presses one end with a foot and the other end lifts, then drops onto the rice. Which simple machine is the dheki?
options: a lever
a pulley
a wedge
a screw
questions.explanation: The beam turns on a pivot, so the dheki is a lever. The heavy head at the far end does the husking.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Which of these are levers? Choose all that are right.
options: a see-saw
a nutcracker
an axe
a jar lid
the handle of a tube-well
questions.explanation: A see-saw, a nutcracker and a tube-well handle all turn on a pivot. An axe is a wedge and a jar lid has a screw thread.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a rickshaw puller starts and then stops the rickshaw.
sequence: The puller pushes the pedals with their feet.
The pedals and crank turn the big gear wheel.
The chain carries the turning to the small gear on the back axle.
The back wheels turn and the rickshaw rolls forward.
The puller squeezes the brake levers, and friction slows the wheels.
questions.explanation: The puller’s push starts the system. The chain carries the turning to the back wheels. Friction from the brake pads on the wheels stops it.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Rahim pushes a heavy box up a ramp instead of lifting it straight up. What does he gain, and what does he give up?
questions.model_answer: He needs a smaller force, but he must push the box a longer distance.
questions.explanation: A ramp makes the job easier because the force is smaller, but the box travels along a longer path.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Which force slows a bicycle down when you squeeze the brake levers?
options: gravity
a magnetic pull
the push from the pedals
friction
questions.explanation: The brake pads press on the wheel and friction slows it. Friction is a force that slows moving things.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: It is easier to open a door by pushing near the handle than by pushing near the hinges.
questions.explanation: The hinge is the pivot. Pushing further from the pivot needs less force, so a door handle is placed far from the hinges.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Look at the picture. Match each letter to the simple machine.
questions.image_alt: Six simple machines lettered A to F.
questions.explanation: The six simple machines are the lever (A), pulley (B), wheel and axle (C), inclined plane or ramp (D), wedge (E) and screw (F).

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Look at the lever. Match each number to its name.
questions.image_alt: A see-saw lever with three parts numbered 1 to 3.
questions.explanation: The effort is the force you put in, the fulcrum (pivot) is the point the lever turns on, and the load is the thing being moved.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Lifting a box straight up needs 10 N. Pulling it up the ramp needs 4 N. How much less force does the ramp need?
questions.image_alt: A box lifted straight up needing 10 N and pulled up a ramp needing 4 N.
options: 4 N
6 N
questions.explanation: 10 N − 4 N = 6 N less force. The ramp path is longer, so the force can be smaller.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: The bucket goes up when the rope is pulled **down**. What job does the pulley do here?
questions.image_alt: A pulley lifting a bucket from a well, and two gears turning each other.
options: It makes the bucket lighter.
It changes the direction of the force.
It removes all the friction.
It makes the rope stronger.
questions.explanation: A fixed pulley does not make the load lighter. It lets you pull down, which is easier than pulling up, to lift the bucket.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: The handle of this tube-well (1) is a lever. Which number is the pivot it turns on?
questions.image_alt: A hand tubewell with parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Number 2 is the pivot. A long handle puts the effort far from the pivot, so less force is needed.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Raju must load a heavy rice sack onto a truck. What is the safest and easiest way?
options: slide it up a long plank used as a ramp
throw it up from the ground
roll it up a short, very steep plank
lift it straight up in one go
questions.explanation: A long, gentle ramp needs a smaller force. A short, steep plank needs more force and is unsafe.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Moung must lift a heavy stone with a crowbar. Where should he push down to need the least force?
options: on the stone itself
close to the pivot
at the far end of the bar
in the middle of the bar
questions.explanation: The further the effort is from the pivot, the less force is needed. That is why crowbars are long.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Nadia’s bicycle takes a long time to stop on wet roads, and her brake pads are worn thin. She should have the pads replaced before riding again.
questions.explanation: Brakes work by friction between the pads and the wheel. Worn pads give less friction, so the bicycle stops too slowly and is unsafe.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Sumi wants to make a cycle rickshaw safer. Which changes would help? Choose all that are right.
options: good brake pads that grip the wheel
bright lights and reflectors
removing the brake levers to save weight
a speed limit for battery rickshaws
smooth tyres with no tread left
questions.explanation: Good brakes use friction to stop the rickshaw, lights help others see it, and a speed limit keeps fast motors safer. Removing brakes or using bald tyres is dangerous.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: A rickshaw puller finds it very hard to go up a bridge with three passengers. Which change in the rickshaw system would help most?
options: using a higher gear to pedal faster
using a lower gear
squeezing the brakes while pedalling
taking the chain off the gears
questions.explanation: A lower gear means a smaller force on the pedals for each turn. Brakes use friction against the movement, and no chain means no drive to the wheels.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: In the simulation, two identical bricks on opposite sides of the pivot, at the same distance, make the plank balance.

sim.task: Open Balancing Act. Drag one brick onto the left side of the plank and a second identical brick onto the right side, at the same distance from the pivot. Look at the plank (take away the supports if you can).

questions.explanation: Equal masses at equal distances from the pivot give equal turning effects, so the plank stays level.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: In the simulation, where must the single brick go to balance the two stacked bricks?

sim.task: Open Balancing Act. Stack two bricks on the left side, close to the pivot. Put one brick on the right side and slide it to different places to find where the plank balances.

options: closer to the pivot than the stack
anywhere on the plank
exactly the same distance as the stack
further from the pivot than the stack
questions.explanation: A lighter load further from the pivot can balance a heavier load closer to it. The same idea explains why a long crowbar helps.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: In the simulation, with the friction slider at none, the crate keeps moving after you stop pushing it.

sim.task: Open Forces and Motion: Basics and choose the Friction screen. Set the friction slider to none. Push the crate with the applied-force slider, then set the push back to zero and watch the crate.

questions.explanation: Without friction nothing slows the crate down. Friction is the force that stops moving things, which is why brakes use it.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: In the simulation, with two large pullers on the left rope and one large puller on the right rope, the cart moves to the left.

sim.task: Open Forces and Motion: Basics and choose the Net Force screen. Put two large pullers on the left (blue) rope and one large puller on the right (red) rope. Press Go.

questions.explanation: The bigger total pull wins. Two large pullers pull with more force than one, so the cart moves left.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Class 5A used a 10 N load, 10 cm from the pivot. Example results: effort 10 N at 10 cm, 5 N at 20 cm, 3.3 N at 30 cm, 2.5 N at 40 cm, 2 N at 50 cm. Predict the effort at 60 cm: about ___ N.
questions.explanation: Each time the distance goes up the effort goes down, and effort × distance stays about 100 (10 × 10). At 60 cm the effort is about 100 ÷ 60 = 1.7 N.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Class 5A’s lever test (10 N load, 10 cm from the pivot) gave: 10 cm needs 10 N, 20 cm needs 5 N, 40 cm needs 2.5 N, 50 cm needs 2 N. Which new readings fit the same pattern? Choose all that are right.
options: 25 cm needs 4 N
40 cm needs 2.5 N
50 cm needs 4 N
5 cm needs 20 N
20 cm needs 8 N
questions.explanation: The effort times the distance is always 100 (10 × 10, 20 × 5, 40 × 2.5). 25 × 4 and 5 × 20 also make 100. 50 × 4 = 200 and 20 × 8 = 160 do not fit.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Example: a 4 kg bag hangs 1 m to the left of the pivot of a plank. A 2 kg bag hangs on the right. Where must it hang to balance the plank?
options: 4 m from the pivot
0.5 m from the pivot
1 m from the pivot
2 m from the pivot
questions.explanation: Half the mass must be twice as far from the pivot: 4 kg × 1 m = 2 kg × 2 m. A 1 m position would make the left side win.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: A car jack lifts a heavy car when you turn its handle many times. Which simple machine does it use and why?
options: a screw, a ramp wrapped round a rod, so many turns make a long path with a small force
a wedge, a sharp edge, so many pushes split the car from the ground
a pulley, a rope round a wheel, so many turns make the car much lighter
a lever, a handle on a pivot, so each turn gives one big push
questions.explanation: A screw is a ramp wrapped around a rod. The long path of many turns means each turn needs only a small force.

questions.title: Mechanical Systems
questions.stem: Use the lever results to explain why a long crowbar helps to lift a heavy stone.
questions.model_answer: A long crowbar lets you push far from the pivot, so you need much less force to lift the heavy stone.
questions.explanation: In the test, the further the effort was from the pivot, the less force was needed. A long crowbar lets you push a long way from the pivot.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Sort these into light sources and things that only reflect light.
questions.explanation: A light source makes its own light. The Moon only reflects sunlight, and a mirror, a page and a spoon reflect light from a source.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: We see a light source, such as a candle flame, when…
options: light from it enters our eyes
it makes the air around it bright
our eyes send rays out to it
it casts a shadow on our eyes
questions.explanation: Seeing happens when light enters the eye. Ibn al-Haytham showed more than 1000 years ago that our eyes do not send out rays.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Our eyes send out rays of light so that we can see things.
questions.explanation: Light comes **into** our eyes, either straight from a source or reflected from an object. In a completely dark room we see nothing.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: The line at right angles to a mirror is called the ___. A mirror image is right way up but back to front, which is called lateral ___.
questions.explanation: Angles of light rays are measured from the normal. Lateral inversion swaps left and right, so your right hand looks like a left hand in a mirror.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Match each optical device to what it does.
pairs: makes an upside-down image through a tiny hole
uses mirrors to make repeating patterns
uses two mirrors to see over a wall
questions.explanation: Each device uses lenses or mirrors to change the way light travels, and so changes the image we see.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: What can happen when light hits a material? Choose all that are right.
options: It is absorbed, so the material looks darker.
It bounces off, so we can see the object.
It turns into sound.
It passes through a transparent material and bends.
It always bounces back exactly the same way, from any surface.
questions.explanation: Light can be absorbed, reflected, or pass through a transparent material and be refracted (bent). Rough surfaces scatter light in many directions instead of one.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how Mina sees a mango on a tree.
sequence: The Sun gives out light.
The light hits the mango.
The mango reflects some of the light.
The light enters Mina’s eye through the pupil.
The retina sends messages along the nerve to her brain.
questions.explanation: The mango is not a light source. We see it because light from the Sun bounces off it and enters the eye.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: A straw in a glass of water looks bent. This is because of…
options: reflection
lateral inversion
absorption
refraction
questions.explanation: Light travels more slowly in water than in air, so it changes direction at the surface. This bending is refraction.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Why does the pupil get smaller when you walk out into bright sunshine?
options: to make the lens bigger
to let less light into the eye
to send light back out
to stop the eyelid closing
questions.explanation: The pupil is a hole that gets smaller in bright light and bigger in the dark. A smaller pupil protects the retina from too much light.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: The word AMBULANCE is painted back to front on the front of an ambulance. Why?
questions.model_answer: A driver in front sees it in the mirror. A mirror reverses left and right (lateral inversion), so the word reads the right way round.
questions.explanation: Mirrors swap left and right. Writing the word back to front means it looks correct in a driver’s mirror.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: A rough surface, such as a rock, scatters light in all directions, so it does not make a clear image.
questions.explanation: Only a very smooth, shiny surface like a mirror reflects light neatly in one direction.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Look at the eye. Match each number to its part.
questions.image_alt: A side view of the eye with parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Light enters through the pupil (2), the lens (3) focuses it on the retina (4), and the optic nerve (5) carries messages to the brain.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Which numbered part focuses light to make a tiny upside-down image on the retina?
questions.image_alt: A side view of the eye with parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is the lens. The retina (4) is where the image forms, and the brain turns it the right way up.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Look at the five devices. Match each letter to its name.
questions.image_alt: Five optical devices lettered A to E.
questions.explanation: These are five optical devices that use lenses, mirrors or a tiny hole to change how we see things.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Which device makes an upside-down image because light travels in straight lines through a tiny hole?
questions.image_alt: Five optical devices lettered A to E.
options: A
C
B
E
questions.explanation: C is the pinhole camera. A is a hand lens, B a telescope and E a kaleidoscope.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: This periscope lets you see over a wall. What does the light do inside it?
questions.image_alt: A periscope with two mirrors at 45 degrees.
options: It is absorbed by the tube.
It bends through a lens.
It reflects off two mirrors.
It travels straight through.
questions.explanation: The two mirrors are set at 45°, so the light turns a right angle at each one: first down the tube, then out to the eye.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: A ray hits the mirror with angle i = 35° to the normal. What is the angle r of the reflected ray?
questions.image_alt: A light ray reflecting off a mirror with the normal, angle i and angle r marked.
questions.explanation: The picture shows that angle i = angle r. The light bounces off at the same angle, measured from the normal.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: A fisherman at a pond sees a fish that looks close to the water surface, but his spear misses. Where should he aim?
options: lower than where the fish seems to be
exactly where the fish seems to be
higher than where the fish seems to be
at the shadow of the boat
questions.explanation: Light from the fish bends as it leaves the water, so the fish looks higher (shallower) than it really is. He must aim lower.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: At lunch, Priya’s friends dare her to look straight at the bright Sun for a few seconds. What should she do?
options: Look quickly through sunglasses
Say no, because it can damage her eyes for ever
Look for just one second
Look only if she squints
questions.explanation: Never look directly at the Sun, even with sunglasses. Its light is strong enough to damage the retina permanently.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Anika has been doing close work on a tablet for 20 minutes. Which habit protects her eyes best?
options: stare at the screen even harder
close one eye and keep reading
hold the tablet closer to her face
look at something about 6 metres away for 20 seconds
questions.explanation: This is the 20-20-20 rule: after every 20 minutes of close work, look about 6 metres (20 feet) away for 20 seconds to rest the eyes.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Joy wants to keep her eyes healthy. Which actions would help? Choose all that are right.
options: play outdoors in daylight every day
follow the 20-20-20 rule on screens
eat vitamin A foods such as spinach, carrots and mango
look at the Sun to make her eyes stronger
skip eye tests even if the board looks blurry
questions.explanation: Daylight outdoors, regular screen breaks and vitamin A foods all help. Looking at the Sun damages the eyes, and blurry sight should always be checked by an eye doctor.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Bangladesh’s national Vitamin A campaign gives capsules to young children to protect them from night blindness.
questions.explanation: Without enough vitamin A people can develop night blindness. Spinach, carrots, mangoes, eggs and small fish like mola are good sources.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the rays from the object when they pass through the convex lens?

sim.task: Open Geometric Optics: Basics and choose the Lens screen. Turn on the rays and move the object to different places. Watch what the rays do as they go through the lens.

options: They pass straight through, unchanged.
They stop at the lens.
They bend as they go into and out of the glass.
They turn into different colours.
questions.explanation: A convex lens refracts light: the rays change direction in the glass, and the bent rays can meet to make an image.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: In the simulation, the rays from the object go through the flat mirror and come out of the other side.

sim.task: Open Geometric Optics: Basics and choose the Mirror screen. Turn on the rays and move the object. Watch where the rays go when they reach the flat mirror.

questions.explanation: A mirror reflects the rays: they bounce off and go back. They do not pass through.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: In the simulation, white light shines through a red filter. Which light comes out?

sim.task: Open Color Vision and choose the Single Bulb screen. Keep the white bulb on and put the red filter in front of it. Look at the colour of the light that comes out.

options: white light, but dimmer
only red light
no light at all
red, green and blue light
questions.explanation: The red filter absorbs the other colours and lets only red light through. The filter is an example of a material that absorbs some light.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Class 5C measured angles of incoming and reflected rays at a mirror. Example results (incoming → reflected): 20° → 20°, 30° → 31°, 40° → 40°, 50° → 56°, 60° → 60°. Which result fits the pattern worst?
questions.explanation: The law of reflection says the two angles are equal. 30° → 31° is only 1° out (a reading error), but 56° is 6° too big, so it is the outlier.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Using the pattern in the class results, a ray arriving at 75° to the normal will be reflected at ___ degrees.
questions.explanation: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so a 75° ray reflects at 75°.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: In the class results the 50° ray was measured as 56° after reflection. Suggest a reason, and say what the class should do.
questions.model_answer: They may have misread the protractor or drawn the normal wrongly, so they should repeat the measurement.
questions.explanation: A result that does not fit is often a measuring slip. Repeating the measurement carefully shows whether it was an error.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Class 5C asked 30 learners about screen time (example data): less than 1 hour 4, 1 to 2 hours 9, 2 to 3 hours 10, more than 3 hours 7. How many learners use screens for 2 hours or more each day? ___
questions.explanation: Add the last two groups: 10 + 7 = 17 learners. The first two groups (4 + 9 = 13) use screens for less than 2 hours.

questions.title: Light: Sources, Reflection and Refraction
questions.stem: Which of these happen because light travels in straight lines? Choose all that are right.
options: A pinhole camera makes an upside-down image.
A periscope needs mirrors to turn light round a corner.
You can see round a corner without a mirror.
The Moon makes its own light.
An opaque object makes a shadow behind it.
questions.explanation: Light goes in straight lines, so a pinhole flips the image, a corner blocks the view unless mirrors turn the light, and opaque objects block light to make shadows. The Moon only reflects sunlight.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Sort the materials into transparent, translucent or opaque.
questions.explanation: Transparent materials let almost all light through. Translucent materials let some through but scatter it. Opaque materials let none through.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Which material would make the darkest shadow?
options: cardboard
tracing paper
clear glass
water
questions.explanation: Cardboard is opaque, so it blocks all the light. Clear glass and water let light pass, and tracing paper lets some through.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Light travels in ___ lines. A shadow forms when an ___ object blocks the light.
questions.explanation: Light cannot bend round an opaque object, so a dark area, the shadow, is left behind it.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: A shadow shows the colours of the object that makes it.
questions.explanation: A shadow shows only the outline shape of the object. It has no colour or detail.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Shadows point towards the Sun.
questions.explanation: The object blocks the light coming from the Sun, so the shadow falls on the side **away** from the Sun.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: lets some light through but scatters it
questions.explanation: These key words describe how materials treat light and how we measure how bright light is.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Why are shadows longer in the morning and evening than at midday?
options: The Sun is brighter.
The shadow is pushed by the wind.
The object grows taller.
The Sun is low in the sky.
questions.explanation: When the Sun is low, its light hits objects at a slant and makes long shadows. At midday the Sun is highest, so shadows are shortest.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Which of these show that light travels in straight lines? Choose all that are right.
options: Sunbeams shine through a gap in the curtains.
A torch beam cuts through mist.
We cannot see round a corner.
Light bends round a wall to fill its shadow.
A sundial works at night.
questions.explanation: Beams, and not being able to see round corners, show straight-line travel. If light bent round objects there would be no shadows.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a shadow puppet’s shadow forms.
sequence: A lamp gives out light.
The light travels in straight lines.
The opaque puppet blocks some of the light.
A dark shape of the puppet appears on the cloth screen.
questions.explanation: Because the light cannot bend round or go through the puppet, the screen behind it stays dark in the shape of the puppet.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Why can you read a book through clear glass but not through tracing paper or cardboard?
questions.model_answer: Clear glass is transparent, so light passes straight through. Tracing paper is translucent and scatters the light so words look blurred. Cardboard is opaque and lets no light through.
questions.explanation: How clearly we see through a material depends on whether it lets light pass straight through, scatters it or blocks it.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: What is the unit of light intensity?
options: decibel
newton
lux
degree
questions.explanation: Light intensity (how bright light is) is measured with a light meter in lux.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Moving an object further from the torch makes its shadow smaller and sharper.
questions.explanation: A nearer object blocks more of the light and makes a bigger shadow. Moving it away makes the shadow smaller and sharper.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Why can you not see a clear shadow on a very cloudy day?
questions.model_answer: Clouds scatter the sunlight, so light comes from all directions and nothing blocks all of it.
questions.explanation: A clear shadow needs light from one direction that an object blocks. Clouds mix the light up so no dark area forms.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.
questions.explanation: Light is very fast, about 300 000 km every second, but the Sun is so far away that its light still takes about 8 minutes to get here.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: The picture shows a stick and its shadow at three times of day. When is the shadow shortest?
questions.image_alt: A stick and its shadow at morning, midday and evening as the Sun moves across the sky.
options: morning
midday
evening
it is always the same
questions.explanation: At midday the Sun is highest in the sky, so the shadow is shortest. In the morning and evening it is long.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Look at the picture. The evening shadow is long because the Sun is low in the sky.
questions.image_alt: A stick and its shadow at morning, midday and evening as the Sun moves across the sky.
questions.explanation: When the Sun is low, objects block its light at a slant and make long shadows. The morning shadow is long for the same reason.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: In the picture the object is moved **closer to the torch**. What happens to the shadow on the screen?
questions.image_alt: A torch, an object and its shadow on a screen.
options: It gets smaller.
It gets bigger.
It disappears.
It changes colour.
questions.explanation: A nearer object blocks more of the light from the torch, so its shadow is bigger (and a little more blurred).

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Without changing the object in the picture, how could you make a different shadow **shape**?
questions.image_alt: A torch, an object and its shadow on a screen.
options: turn or tilt the object
move the screen away
use a brighter torch
make the room darker
questions.explanation: The shadow is the outline of the object as seen from the light. Turning or tilting the object changes the outline, so the shape changes.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Why is there a dark shadow on the screen in the picture?
questions.image_alt: A torch, an object and its shadow on a screen.
options: The torch gives out dark light.
The screen absorbs all the light.
The opaque object blocks the light.
The object makes its own darkness.
questions.explanation: Light cannot go through an opaque object or bend round it, so the screen behind it receives no light.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Rafi is putting on a shadow puppet show with a lamp and a cloth screen. How can he make a puppet’s shadow bigger?
options: use a coloured paper puppet
move it closer to the screen
move it further from the lamp
move it closer to the lamp
questions.explanation: The closer the puppet is to the lamp, the more light it blocks and the bigger the shadow. Colour makes no difference to a shadow.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: A hot Dhaka classroom has glare near the windows and a dark back corner. Which ideas would help make it brighter and cooler? Choose all that are right.
options: paint the walls and ceiling white
use translucent blinds on the windows
plant trees outside the windows
paint the walls black
close thick curtains all day
questions.explanation: White surfaces reflect light round the room. Translucent blinds let light in but cut glare and heat. Trees block direct sun. Black walls and thick curtains make the room darker.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: A light meter shows 120 lux at the back corner of a classroom. Experts recommend 300 to 500 lux for reading, so this corner is too dim.
questions.explanation: 120 lux is well below 300 lux. Too little light strains the eyes, so learners at the back may need more light or a better seat.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: The school has a sundial. Why does its shadow move round during the day?
options: The stick slowly turns round on the ground.
The wind pushes the shadow round the stick.
The Sun seems to move as the Earth spins.
The Sun gets bigger and then smaller.
questions.explanation: Shadows always point away from the Sun. As the Sun seems to move from east to west, the shadow moves round, so the sundial can tell the time.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Joy wants a lampshade that gives soft light, not a harsh glare. Which material is best?
options: a steel tray
thin cotton cloth
cardboard
clear glass
questions.explanation: Thin cotton cloth is translucent, so it lets some light through but scatters it. Steel and cardboard block it, and clear glass lets a harsh glare through.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Anika says one window gives more light than another. Measuring both with a light meter app is fairer than saying "it looks quite bright".
questions.explanation: A light meter gives a number in lux, so the results can be compared and checked by other people.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Nadia measured a 1 m stick’s shadow in the school yard (example data): 8 am 210 cm, 10 am 80 cm, 12 noon 30 cm, 2 pm 75 cm, 4 pm 190 cm. Which conclusions are supported? Choose all that are right.
options: The shadow was shortest at 12 noon.
The 8 am shadow was more than twice as long as the 10 am shadow.
The shadows at 10 am and 2 pm were exactly the same length.
Thicker sticks make shorter shadows.
The shadow got longer between 2 pm and 4 pm.
questions.explanation: 30 cm is the smallest. 210 ÷ 80 is about 2.6, so more than double. 80 cm and 75 cm are close but not equal, and the test did not compare different sticks.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: Jamal held a 10 cm puppet at different distances from a torch, with a screen 60 cm away (example data): 10 cm → shadow 60 cm; 20 cm → 30 cm; 30 cm → 20 cm; 40 cm → 15 cm; 50 cm → 12 cm. Predict the shadow height with the puppet 15 cm from the torch: about ___ cm.
questions.explanation: The closer the puppet, the taller the shadow. Distance × shadow height is always 600 (10 × 60, 20 × 30, 30 × 20…), so at 15 cm the shadow is 600 ÷ 15 = 40 cm.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: In Jamal’s test, which change would make the test unfair?
options: using a bigger puppet for the 30 cm trial
using the same torch every time
keeping the screen 60 cm from the torch
measuring the shadow height each time
questions.explanation: Only the distance from the torch may change. A different puppet size would change the shadow too, so we could not tell what caused the difference.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: In 1676 Ole Rømer noticed that one of Jupiter’s moons appeared from behind the planet later than expected when Earth was further away. What did this show about light?
questions.model_answer: Light takes time to travel. When Earth was further away, the light had further to go, so it arrived later.
questions.explanation: People once thought light arrived instantly. Rømer’s observation showed that light has a speed, so a longer distance means a longer travel time.

questions.title: Light: Shadows and Intensity
questions.stem: A well-lit classroom has 300 to 500 lux. A sunny day outdoors has 50 000 to 100 000 lux. At the very least, how many times brighter is a sunny day than the brightest well-lit classroom?
options: 10 times
1000 times
100 times
10 000 times
questions.explanation: Compare the lowest sunny value with the highest classroom value: 50 000 ÷ 500 = 100. So a sunny day is at least 100 times brighter.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Which kind of heat transfer is it? Sort the examples.
items: a metal pan handle gets hot
feet feel cold on a tiled floor
warm air rises from a heater
you feel warm in front of a fire
questions.explanation: Conduction passes heat through solids by touch. Convection is warm air or liquid rising. Radiation is heat travelling as invisible infrared rays, even through space.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Sort these materials into good conductors and good insulators of heat.
questions.explanation: Metals let heat through easily. Wool, wood and especially trapped air slow the flow of heat.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth through empty space. How does it travel?
options: by conduction
by radiation
by convection
by evaporation
questions.explanation: Radiation does not need particles, so infrared rays can cross empty space. Conduction and convection need particles.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: In a solid, heat passes from particle to particle by ___. In liquids and gases, warm parts rise in a loop called ___.
questions.explanation: Conduction needs touching particles in a solid. Convection is the loop of rising warm and sinking cool fluid.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: A big bucket of warm water holds more heat than a small cup of boiling water.
questions.explanation: Temperature tells us how hot something is, but heat depends on how much material there is as well. The bucket has many more particles holding energy.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Trapped air is a good insulator, which is why a woollen jumper keeps you warm.
questions.explanation: Wool traps many tiny pockets of air. Trapped air slows the movement of heat away from your body.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Explain, using particles, why a metal spoon in hot dal gets hot all the way up to the handle.
questions.model_answer: The particles at the hot end vibrate faster and bump into their neighbours, passing energy along the metal to the handle. This is conduction, and metal is a good conductor.
questions.explanation: In a solid the particles are close together, so hotter, faster-vibrating particles quickly pass energy to their neighbours.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Which parts of a vacuum flask slow down heat transfer? Choose all that are right.
options: the vacuum between the walls
the shiny silver walls
the stopper
a dark, dull inner wall
a thin metal base touching the table
questions.explanation: The vacuum has no particles, so no conduction or convection. Shiny walls reflect radiation. The stopper stops warm air escaping by convection.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a convection current forms in a pot of water on a stove.
sequence: The stove heats the water at the bottom.
The warm water expands and becomes less dense.
The warm water rises.
Cooler, denser water sinks to take its place.
A loop of moving water forms: a convection current.
questions.explanation: Warm liquid is less dense and rises, and cooler, denser liquid sinks. The moving loop stirs the whole pot.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Match each key word to its meaning.
pairs: heat passing through a solid, particle to particle
heat carried by a moving liquid or gas
questions.explanation: These five words describe how heat moves and how materials handle it.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: In which direction does heat move?
options: from hotter things to colder things
only through metals
only upwards
from colder things to hotter things
questions.explanation: Heat is energy that moves because of a temperature difference, from hot to cold, until the temperatures are the same.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: A cook’s pan has a copper base and a plastic handle. Explain both choices.
questions.model_answer: Copper is a good conductor, so it passes heat quickly to the food. Plastic is an insulator, so the handle stays cool to hold.
questions.explanation: Pans need heat to flow into the food, so the base is a conductor. The handle must slow heat flow, so it is an insulator.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Look at the three pictures. Match each letter to the way heat travels.
questions.image_alt: Three pictures lettered A, B and C: a spoon in a hot drink, a pot of water over a flame with arrows, and the Sun warming a hand.
questions.explanation: A: a spoon in a hot drink gets hot by conduction. B: water moves in a loop over the flame (convection). C: the Sun warms a hand by radiation.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: In picture B, why does the warm water at the bottom of the pot rise?
questions.image_alt: Three pictures lettered A, B and C: a spoon in a hot drink, a pot of water over a flame with arrows, and the Sun warming a hand.
options: It becomes heavier than the cool water.
It is pushed up by the spoon.
It expands and becomes less dense.
It turns into the flame.
questions.explanation: Warm water expands, so it is less dense than the cooler water around it and floats upwards. Cooler, denser water sinks to take its place.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: In the vacuum flask, which number is the **vacuum**, the empty space between the walls?
questions.image_alt: A vacuum flask cut in half with parts numbered 1 to 5.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is the vacuum. It has no particles, so heat cannot cross it by conduction or convection.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Which part of the flask reflects heat radiation back towards the hot drink?
questions.image_alt: A vacuum flask cut in half with parts numbered 1 to 5.
options: number 1, the stopper
number 4, the hot drink
number 5, the outer case
number 2, the shiny silver walls
questions.explanation: Shiny surfaces reflect radiation, so the silver walls (2) send heat back instead of letting it escape. The stopper (1) stops warm air rising out.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Four cups hold the same hot water. Which cup will cool down the fastest?
questions.image_alt: Four cups of hot water: no cover, newspaper, wool and foil.
options: the cup with no cover
the cup wrapped in wool
the cup wrapped in newspaper
the cup wrapped in foil
questions.explanation: Without a cover there is nothing to slow the heat loss. Newspaper and wool are insulators, and foil reflects radiation.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Where should a room heater be placed to warm the whole room best?
options: near the ceiling
right next to the door
inside a cupboard
near the floor
questions.explanation: Warm air rises, so a low heater sets up a convection current: warm air goes up and cooler air sinks to be warmed.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: It is a very sunny day in Dhaka. Which shirt will keep Rafi coolest?
options: a black cotton shirt
a dark blue woollen shirt
a light-coloured cotton shirt
a dark nylon shirt
questions.explanation: Light colours reflect more of the Sun’s radiation and absorb less heat, so they stay cooler than dark clothes.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Mina wants her rice to stay warm for four hours on a school trip. Which is the best choice?
options: an open metal bowl
a tightly closed container wrapped in a woollen cloth
a metal tin with its lid off
a bowl placed on a cold stone
questions.explanation: A lid stops warm air escaping by convection, and wool is an insulator that slows conduction. An open metal bowl loses heat quickly.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Many homes in Dhaka have thin tin roofs that get very hot in the sun. Which ideas would help cool the room below? Choose all that are right.
options: paint the roof white
add a jute or bamboo ceiling with an air gap
grow creepers or trees for shade
paint the roof black
take the ceiling out
questions.explanation: White paint reflects radiation, jute and trapped air are insulators, and shade blocks the Sun. A black roof absorbs more heat, and removing a ceiling removes insulation.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Before lifting a hot metal pan from the stove, Sumi should use a cloth or oven glove, because metal conducts heat quickly.
questions.explanation: Metal is a good conductor, so a hot pan handle can burn bare hands. Cloth is an insulator and protects the skin.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: In the simulation, the thermometer reading goes up while the burner heats the water.

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Intro screen. Put the beaker of water over a burner, slide the burner to heat, and watch the thermometer.

questions.explanation: Heat from the burner makes the water particles move faster, so the temperature rises.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: In the simulation, a hot iron block touches a cooler brick block. What happens to their temperatures?

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Intro screen. Heat the iron block with a burner, then move it so that it touches the cooler brick block. Watch both thermometers.

options: Both stay exactly the same.
The iron cools down and the brick warms up.
The iron gets hotter and the brick colder.
The brick cools down and the iron warms up.
questions.explanation: Heat flows from the hotter object to the colder one by conduction, until they reach about the same temperature.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: In the simulation, when the burner is slid to the cooling side under the water, the thermometer reading goes down.

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Intro screen. Slide the burner under the beaker of water to the cooling side and watch the thermometer.

questions.explanation: Cooling takes heat energy out of the water, so its particles slow down and the temperature falls.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Class 5B wrapped three cans of water in black paper, white paper and shiny foil and put them in the sun (example data). After 40 minutes: black 45 °C, white 35 °C, foil 32 °C, all starting at 28 °C. The black can ended ___ °C hotter than the foil can.
questions.explanation: 45 − 32 = 13 °C. Dark, dull surfaces absorb radiation best, and shiny foil reflects most of it.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Use the can results (start 28 °C; after 40 minutes black 45 °C, white 35 °C, foil 32 °C). Which conclusions are supported? Choose all that are right.
options: The black can warmed the most.
The shiny foil can warmed the least.
The white can warmed faster than the black can.
Dark colours would keep a can cooler in the sun.
The white can rose by 7 °C in 40 minutes.
questions.explanation: Black rose 17 °C, white 7 °C and foil 4 °C. Dark colours absorb more radiation, so they heat up faster, not stay cooler.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: A community group measured four rooms at 2 pm (example data): bare tin roof 41 °C, white-painted roof 36 °C, jute ceiling with air gap 35 °C, tree shade + white roof 32 °C. How much cooler was the best room than the bare tin roof room?
questions.explanation: 41 − 32 = 9 °C. The shade stops radiation reaching the roof and the white paint reflects the rest.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Design a lunch box that keeps rice hot for four hours. Say how it reduces conduction, convection **and** radiation.
questions.model_answer: Double walls with an air gap or a wool cover reduce conduction. A tight lid stops warm air escaping, which reduces convection. A shiny inner lining reflects radiation.
questions.explanation: Each part tackles one kind of heat transfer: insulators slow conduction, a lid stops convection and shiny surfaces reflect radiation, just like a vacuum flask.

questions.title: Heat Transfer: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
questions.stem: Which statement about heat and temperature is correct?
options: Hot things always hold more heat than cooler things.
Temperature and heat are two names for the same thing.
A thermometer measures how much heat an object holds.
A bucket of warm water holds more heat than a cup of boiling water.
questions.explanation: Temperature is how hot something is. Heat depends on temperature and on how much material there is, so a large bucket can hold more heat than a small cup.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Sort these energy resources into renewable and non-renewable.
questions.explanation: Renewable resources are replaced by nature and will not run out. Coal, oil and natural gas took millions of years to form, and uranium (nuclear fuel) is also limited.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Natural gas is a renewable resource.
questions.explanation: Natural gas is a fossil fuel. It formed over millions of years and we use it much faster than it forms, so it will run out.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Burning fossil fuels releases ___ ___ (CO₂), a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the air.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide traps heat, so more of it in the air leads to climate change.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: A renewable energy resource is one that…
options: formed from buried plants over millions of years
is made in a factory and sold in shops
is replaced naturally and will not run out
can be used only once by one power station
questions.explanation: Sunlight, wind and moving water are renewable. The resource formed from buried plants over millions of years describes a fossil fuel, which is non-renewable.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Match each energy resource to what it comes from.
pairs: plants buried for millions of years
questions.explanation: Renewable resources come from the Sun, the wind, water, living things or heat inside the Earth. Coal is a fossil fuel made from plants buried for millions of years.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Nuclear power stations release a lot of carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: They release almost none. But nuclear fuel (uranium) is non-renewable and the waste is dangerous.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Which of these are green energy choices? Choose all that are right.
options: solar panels
wind turbines
burning more coal
LED bulbs that use less energy
leaving fans on in empty rooms
questions.explanation: Solar and wind release little or no pollution, and using energy efficiently is green too. Burning coal and wasting electricity do the opposite.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how burning fossil fuels causes climate change.
sequence: Coal, oil or gas is burned.
Carbon dioxide is released into the air.
The extra carbon dioxide traps more heat.
The Earth warms and the climate changes.
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide trap heat, so more of them means a warmer Earth, with changes such as stronger cyclones and rising seas.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Why is burning fossil fuels a **global** problem?
options: It only harms the town where the fuel is burned.
The carbon dioxide spreads through the air and affects the whole planet.
It makes all the fuel renewable.
It makes the air colder everywhere.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide from any country mixes in the air and traps heat everywhere. That is why countries must act together.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Why is Bangladesh one of the countries most at risk from climate change?
questions.model_answer: Climate change brings stronger cyclones, floods and rising sea levels, and Bangladesh is low and has a long coast.
questions.explanation: Bangladesh faces stronger cyclones, floods and sea-level rise along the coast, which put homes, farms and lives at risk.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: About 685 million people in the world still had no electricity at home in 2022 (Tracking SDG7). In which region do most of them live?
options: Sub-Saharan Africa
North America
Australia
Europe
questions.explanation: Most people without electricity live in Sub-Saharan Africa. Energy access is a global issue as well as a climate issue.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Which picture shows a source of green energy?
questions.explanation: Wind turbines use renewable wind and release no smoke. The other pictures show pollution from burning or using fossil fuels.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Match each picture to the energy it uses.
questions.explanation: Solar, wind and hydro use sunlight, moving air and moving water. A nuclear power station uses uranium, which is non-renewable.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Which pictures show things that put smoke or fumes into the air? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Factories and cars burning fossil fuels release smoke, fumes and carbon dioxide. Solar panels, wind turbines and bicycles do not.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Which picture shows a hazard that climate change is making worse for Bangladesh?
questions.explanation: Climate change brings stronger cyclones, floods and sea-level rise to Bangladesh. Volcanoes, snow and deserts are not the main risks.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: A hydro power station makes electricity using which of these?
questions.explanation: Hydro means water. Moving water turns a generator to make electricity, as at the Kaptai plant on the Karnaphuli River.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Rafi’s school wants to cut its electricity bill. Which change helps most without lowering learning?
options: leave the lights on all day
swap old bulbs for LED bulbs
run the computers overnight
buy more fans and keep them on
questions.explanation: LED bulbs give the same light with less electricity. The cleanest energy is the energy we do not waste.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: A family on a remote char far from the national grid wants clean electricity for lights and a phone charger. What is a good choice?
options: a coal-fired generator
a big hydro dam
a solar home system
a nuclear power station
questions.explanation: Solar home systems use sunlight, release no pollution, and are already used by millions of homes in Bangladesh. The other options are far too large or polluting for one family.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Anika switches off the fan and lights when she leaves an empty classroom. This saves electricity and helps to cut carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: Much of our electricity still comes from fossil fuels. Using less electricity means less fuel is burned.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: The school wants to cut its electricity bill and its carbon footprint. Which actions would help? Choose all that are right.
options: put solar panels on the roof
use LED bulbs
switch off fans and lights in empty rooms
leave the computers on overnight
use old bulbs that waste more energy
questions.explanation: Solar panels give clean electricity, and LED bulbs and switching off save energy. Leaving things on or using wasteful bulbs does the opposite.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Nadia’s family in a village keeps cows. How could they get a renewable fuel for cooking?
options: collecting natural gas from the ground
burning plastic bottles
buying coal from the market
a biogas plant that uses dung
questions.explanation: Biogas is made from animal dung and plants, so it can be replaced all the time. Coal and natural gas are fossil fuels, and burning plastic is harmful.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the temperature when you add more greenhouse gases to the air?

sim.task: Open Greenhouse Effect. Turn on the sunlight. Watch the thermometer, then add more greenhouse gases to the air and watch again.

options: It goes up.
It goes down.
It stays exactly the same.
It goes up and then falls back to zero.
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases trap heat that tries to escape from the ground, so the air warms. This is why burning fossil fuels causes climate change.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: In the simulation, with more greenhouse gases in the air, more of the heat (infrared) rising from the ground is trapped instead of escaping.

sim.task: Open Greenhouse Effect. Turn on the sunlight. Compare the heat (infrared) rays leaving the ground with only a little gas in the air and with a lot of greenhouse gas.

questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases absorb the heat rays and send some back down. More gas means more heat is trapped.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Put the energy chain in order for a solar panel lighting a bulb.

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Systems screen. Choose the Sun as the source, a solar panel as the energy changer and a light bulb as the user. Watch where the energy goes.

sequence: Sunlight shines on the solar panel.
The solar panel changes the light into electricity.
Electricity flows to the light bulb.
The bulb gives out light.
questions.explanation: The Sun is the energy source, the solar panel changes the energy, and the bulb uses it. Sunlight is a renewable resource.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: In the simulation, running water turns the generator and the light bulb lights up. Which kind of power station does this copy?

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Systems screen. Choose the tap with running water as the source, the generator as the energy changer and a light bulb as the user. Watch the generator and the bulb.

options: a solar power station
a hydro power station
a nuclear power station
a coal power station
questions.explanation: Moving water turns the generator, just as in a hydro plant like Kaptai. Water is a renewable resource.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: World electricity in 2024 (Ember, rounded): coal 34%, gas 22%, other fossil 3%, nuclear 9%, hydro 14%, wind 8%, solar 7%, other renewable 3%. Which statements are right? Choose all that are right.
options: Fossil fuels together made about 59%.
Wind and solar together made more electricity than hydro.
Nuclear and all renewables together made about 41%.
Gas made more electricity than coal.
Hydro, wind, solar and other renewables together made more than coal.
questions.explanation: 34 + 22 + 3 = 59%. Wind + solar = 15%, which is more than hydro (14%). Nuclear 9 + renewables 32 = 41%. Coal (34%) beat gas (22%), and renewables (32%) were just below coal.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Bangladesh made 55% of its electricity from natural gas, 20% from oil, 14% from coal and 11% from imports, hydro and solar (2023, PGCB data reported by Reuters). The world made 22% from gas and 34% from coal (2024, Ember). Which comparison is correct?
options: Bangladesh made over half its electricity from renewables.
Bangladesh used a bigger share of coal than the world did.
Bangladesh used a bigger share of gas than the world did.
The world made most of its electricity from gas.
questions.explanation: 55% is bigger than 22% for gas. For coal, Bangladesh (14%) used a smaller share than the world (34%). Neither made most of its electricity from renewables.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: In 2023 Bangladesh made 55% of its electricity from natural gas, 20% from oil and 14% from coal (PGCB data reported by Reuters). Together, fossil fuels made ___ % of its electricity.
questions.explanation: 55 + 20 + 14 = 89%. Only about 11% came from imports, hydro and solar, so Bangladesh depends heavily on fossil fuels.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Class 5A tested a paper wind turbine with 6 blades in front of a fan (example data). The turns in 30 seconds were 52, 55 and 55. The mean number of turns is ___.
questions.explanation: 52 + 55 + 55 = 162, and 162 ÷ 3 = 54. Repeating a test and finding the mean makes results more reliable.

questions.title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy
questions.stem: Class 5A’s mean turns in 30 seconds (example data): 2 blades 40, 3 blades 56, 4 blades 61, 6 blades 54, 8 blades 44. Describe the pattern and explain why more blades are not always better.
questions.model_answer: The speed rose up to 4 blades and then fell. More blades catch more wind, but too many add weight and block the air.
questions.explanation: The best result was 61 turns with 4 blades. After that extra blades made the turbine heavier and got in each other’s way, so it turned more slowly.
